sections.heading: Purpose and scope
sections.text: This document describes the reference data set (RDS) RDS-CCF-REV-3.0 used to develop and calibrate the conversion factor model CCF-REV v3.0 (inventory identifier MDL-03) for the Bank's retail revolving exposures: credit cards and arranged current account overdrafts granted to natural persons in the Netherlands. The model estimates the conversion factor (CCF) applied to the undrawn part of committed revolving limits in the calculation of exposure values under the Advanced IRB approach, in accordance with CRR Articles 166(8a) to 166(8c) and 182. The rating system is used within the Bank's IRB permission for the retail exposure class (qualifying revolving retail and other retail exposures), which has been approved since 2008; the experience test of CRR Article 145 is therefore met for the range of application of this rating system. The document follows the RDS documentation template of MRM-STD-021 Annex A, is stored in the controlled document repository linked to the model inventory (DocHub folder MDL-03/RDS) and is subject to version control with a document history in section 9. Cover block: title CCF RDS documentation; model CCF-REV v3.0 (MDL-03); document version 0.8; status draft for review; author S. Bakker (Retail Credit Risk Modelling); reviewer J. Visser; approver M. de Vries, Model Owner and Director Retail Credit Risk; not yet approved.

sections.heading: Observation period
sections.text: The RDS covers all default events with a default date between 1 January 2012 and 31 December 2025 on credit card and overdraft facilities, each linked to the monthly account snapshot at the reference date twelve months before default; the underlying account panel therefore starts on 1 January 2011. The base panel contains 282.4 million account-month records for 1,934,700 unique facilities of 1,512,300 unique obligors, and the frozen RDS contains 133,211 default events (56,480 credit card and 76,731 overdraft events). With fourteen years of default dates, the observation period exceeds the minimum of five years required for retail conversion factors by CRR Article 182(3) and CRM-STD-100 §6.2. Snapshots are taken at each month-end from the Retail Data Warehouse (RDW); the default events are sourced from the Bank's default register and are available with a daily default date.

sections.heading: Choice of observation window
sections.text: The window starts in January 2012 because complete monthly limit and balance histories for credit cards are available from January 2011 onwards, which is the earliest possible reference date for a twelve-month fixed horizon; earlier card data were held by the previous processor and were not migrated at transaction level. The window covers the Dutch recession of 2012–2013 with the unemployment peak of early 2014, the benign years 2015–2019, the COVID-19 period 2020–2021 with extensive government support and the inflation shock of 2022–2023, and therefore contains a mix of economic conditions relevant for current and foreseeable conditions. Two system migrations fall in the window: the migration of current accounts from the legacy core banking system CBS-L to Core24 in October 2014 and the change of card processor in March 2017; both are treated in section 6.2 (deficiencies DD-CCF-02 and DD-CCF-04). The identification of the economic downturn relevant for conversion factors and its coverage by the window are documented in the downturn report EVD-03-DT and summarised in MDD chapter 5. All defaults from the window are used; no sub-period is excluded, so that the long-run average reflects all observed defaults in the data sources.

sections.heading: Target variable and outcome horizon
sections.text: The target variable is the realised conversion factor of each defaulted facility, calculated with a fixed horizon of twelve months: CCF = (EAD at default − drawn amount at reference date) / (limit at reference date − drawn amount at reference date), where the reference date is the month-end snapshot twelve months before the default date. The EAD at default is the outstanding balance on the default date including capitalised interest and fees; drawings, interest and fees after the default date are not part of the realised CCF and are captured in the realised LGD of the retail revolving LGD model (MDL-04), in line with CRM-STD-100 §10.2. Realised CCFs are not capped at 100%, and the EAD at default is not capped at the limit or at the principal amount outstanding, so that over-limit drawings, capitalised interest and fees are fully reflected in the RDS. Where a facility was opened less than twelve months before default, the snapshot at the end of the month of origination is used as reference date; this applies to 3,912 events (2.9%) and is recorded in the RDS field ref_date_type. Facilities whose drawn amount equalled or exceeded the limit at the reference date (undrawn amount ≤ 0) have an undefined realised CCF; the 1,954 events concerned are kept in the RDS with their realised additional drawings but are not used in the average realised CCF (see DD-CCF-03).

sections.heading: Default definition – days past due and materiality threshold
sections.text: An obligor is in default when it is more than 90 days past due on a material credit obligation or is considered unlikely to pay; any amount of principal, interest or fee not paid on its due date is recognised as past due. The materiality threshold is the one set by the ECB for all significant institutions under Delegated Regulation (EU) 2018/171: EUR 100 absolute and 1% relative for retail exposures. The absolute component is compared with the sum of all amounts past due owed by the obligor to the Bank and its subsidiaries, and the relative component divides that sum by the obligor's total on-balance-sheet exposure excluding equity exposures. The days-past-due counter starts on the first day on which both components are exceeded and restarts when either component is no longer exceeded; default under the past due criterion occurs on the 91st consecutive day, and no months-in-arrears proxy is used. Where a repayment schedule is modified, days past due are counted on the modified schedule, and payment holidays granted under contractual rights or by law (including the COVID-19 moratoria of 2020) were not counted as past due but were screened for unlikeliness to pay. Counting is suspended for disputed amounts only when the dispute is before a court or the Dutch financial services complaints institute Kifid; 212 such cases are flagged in the RDS. All thresholds are denominated in euro and all exposures in scope are euro-denominated, so the currency provision of Article 5 of the RTS does not apply.

sections.heading: Default definition – level of application and date of default
sections.text: Default is applied at obligor level for all retail exposures in line with the Bank's risk management practice (CR-STD-110 §4.2): when an obligor defaults, all its credit obligations, including cards and overdrafts not in arrears, are flagged as defaulted in all systems. The option to apply the definition at facility level for retail exposures is not used, so no facility-level threshold is applied and the facility-level threshold test does not arise. Because the definition is applied at obligor level, the materiality threshold is calculated at obligor level, and a joint obligor (for example a joint current account of two partners) is treated as a separate obligor in the threshold calculation; the default of a joint obligation leads to default of the individual exposures of both co-obligors unless the exceptions of paragraph 97 of EBA/GL/2016/07 apply. The date of default is the first day on which any default criterion is met; dpd counters are calculated daily in the collections system CollectPlus, so the date of default equals the date the past due criterion was actually fulfilled. Default identification is consistent across the card processor feed, Core24 and the mortgage and consumer loan systems through the Group customer identifier, so a default of the obligor on any product is flagged on the credit card and overdraft facilities without undue delay. There are no legal impediments to data exchange between the Bank and its consumer credit subsidiary, so the inconsistency described in paragraph 81 of EBA/GL/2016/07 does not arise.

sections.heading: Default definition – probation periods and multiple defaults
sections.text: An obligor returns to non-default status only when no default trigger has applied for at least three months and the assessment of its behaviour and financial situation shows that the improvement is factual and permanent; after a distressed restructuring the probation period is at least twelve months and requires a material payment, no amount past due and no concerns about full repayment. The probation start date and status are stored for every default event in the fields prob_start_dt and prob_status. Where an obligor defaults again within twelve months of returning to non-default status, both events are merged into one default event starting on the first default date; 5,218 facility events were merged in this way and the merged events keep the reference date of the first default. Re-default rates are analysed annually by default trigger: of the obligors cured in 2022–2024, 8.7% re-defaulted within twelve months (forbearance-related cures: 17.4%), which the Credit Risk Management annual review of 2025 judged acceptable without extending the probation period.

sections.heading: Unlikeliness-to-pay triggers – automatic triggers
sections.text: The following UTP triggers lead to default automatically: non-accrued status; specific credit risk adjustment or IFRS 9 Stage 3 classification; sale of a credit obligation at a credit-related economic loss above 5%; distressed restructuring with a diminished financial obligation above 1%; bankruptcy or admission to the statutory debt restructuring scheme (WSNP); and charge-off of the account. Specific credit risk adjustments are UTP indications only where they result from a significant perceived decline in credit quality; the collective allowances for Stage 1 and Stage 2 are not treated as UTP. The diminished financial obligation is calculated as (NPV0 − NPV1)/NPV0 with cash flows discounted at the original effective interest rate; forborne facilities below the 1% threshold are assessed for other UTP indications such as repeated forbearance or a large final instalment, and all forborne non-performing exposures are classified as defaulted. Charged-off unsecured retail claims are periodically sold to debt purchasers after default; the loss on sale L = (E − P)/E is calculated per sale, sales above the 5% threshold are recorded as defaults at the moment of sale where default had not been recognised before, and the reasons for each sale are documented by Collections. Automatic triggers are evaluated daily, and a monthly control compares the forborne non-performing list with the default register to verify that all such exposures are flagged as defaulted.

sections.heading: Unlikeliness-to-pay triggers – case-by-case indicators
sections.text: Additional UTP indicators for retail revolving exposures (fraud by the customer, significant loss of income reported to Collections, multiple forbearance within 24 months, BKR negative registration at another lender) lead to a case-by-case assessment by the Collections expert team, completed within 30 days of detection and recorded with its rationale. For each indicator the identification method, information source and monitoring frequency are defined in the UTP operating procedure (Collections procedure COL-P-014 v5), which maps each trigger to source-system fields and assigns responsibilities. Technical past due situations are recognised only for Bank data or system errors, payment execution failures and payment allocation time lags; they are documented and corrected within 30 days, and the 2,114 technical past due events identified in the default register are removed from the RDS. Because UTP labels are set partly by human judgement, the labelling guideline of COL-P-014 is applied by the central Collections team only, and a semi-annual analysis compares UTP rates per assessor; the 2025 analysis found no systematic differences between assessors (chi-square p = 0.41). Contagion between connected retail obligors is limited to joint credit obligations as described in section 3.3.2; no further group-of-connected-clients contagion applies to natural persons in scope.

sections.heading: Data sources
sections.text: The RDS is built from five source systems: the card processor files delivered monthly by CardServ B.V. (card limits, balances, transactions), the current account system Core24 and its predecessor CBS-L (overdraft limits and balances), the collections system CollectPlus (daily arrears and dpd counters), the default register DefaultHub maintained under CR-STD-110, and the finance ledger (write-offs and reconciliation totals). Each source belongs to a data domain with exactly one Data Owner recorded in the Group Data Catalogue: Cards (Head of Retail Cards), Payments and Accounts (Head of Daily Banking), Collections (Head of Retail Collections), Credit Risk Data (Director Credit Risk Management) and Finance Data (Head of Financial Reporting). The authoritative source for every data type is defined: CardServ for card balances and limits, Core24 for overdraft balances and limits, DefaultHub for default status and dates, and the finance ledger for write-offs. Card processing is performed by the third party CardServ B.V. under an outsourcing agreement; the Bank retains full responsibility for the data, receives the complete monthly account file, reconciles it with the ledger and has contractual access rights to transaction-level data, and the third-party involvement is recorded in the outsourcing register (OR-2017-022). No external or pooled data are used in the RDS; the provisions on external data, pooled data and the adjustment of external default definitions are therefore not applicable.

sections.heading: Lineage and critical data elements
sections.text: Lineage from the source systems to the RDS is documented for every variable in RDS Annex A, identifying the source table and field, each intermediate store (RDW staging, RDW core, model data store), every transformation, filter, join and aggregation with a reference to the build script and line range, and the extraction frequency and timing. Discarded variables that were used to construct retained variables, such as the daily balance history used to derive the maximum balance before default, are included in the lineage. For the card processor data the lineage starts at the point of receipt in the Bank's secure file gateway and records the provider, the data product (monthly account master file ACCMAST) and the delivery date of each file. All model input variables and all data elements used to construct the target variable (limit and drawn amount at the reference date, balance at default, default flag and default date) are designated critical data elements, each with a business definition, a technical definition and DQ rules per applicable dimension. The lineage was updated in March 2026 to reflect the replacement of the RDW staging layer, before the changed data were used in development, and the Data Owners confirmed that no change to definitions or transformation logic of these elements is planned without prior notice to the Model Owner. Aggregation is fully automated; the only manual interventions in the data flow are the expert mapping of 43 legacy CBS-L product codes to current products and the list of disputed accounts, both held as version-controlled input files and identified explicitly in the lineage with their four-eyes control.

sections.heading: Exclusions
sections.text: Exclusions are applied in the following order, each with a documented reason approved by the Model Owner on 12 June 2026 (approval record in ticket CRMRET-2214). E1 – technical past due events: 2,114 events (1.5% of the 141,164 events after merging multiple defaults; 1,037 credit card, 1,077 overdraft), removed because they are not defaults. E2 – facilities without a committed limit at the reference date (tolerated, unarranged overdrafts and cancelled card limits): 4,806 events (3.4%; 4,211 overdraft, 595 credit card), removed because no undrawn commitment exists to which a CCF can be applied; their exposure value equals the drawn amount. E3 – duplicate facility records created by the Core24 migration in October 2014: 1,033 events (0.7%, all overdraft), removed after matching legacy and new account numbers. In the overdraft segment the exclusions sum to 6.1% of events, which exceeds the 5% threshold of MRM-STD-022 §5.3; the exclusions were therefore approved by the Model Owner and reported to Model Validation on 12 June 2026. For each exclusion the conclusion of the impact analysis is stated in section 5.3: none of the exclusions changes the average realised CCF of any segment by more than 0.4 percentage points.

sections.heading: Missing values and outliers
sections.text: The treatment of missing values is documented per variable in RDS Annex C, distinguishing values missing at random, missing for a structural reason (for example no previous limit change for new accounts) and missing because of a data deficiency. The only imputation concerns the overdraft limit at the reference date for 2,904 overdraft events in 2012–2014 whose limit history was not migrated from CBS-L; the limit is reconstructed from the product parameter table and the customer's limit at migration, is flagged in the field lim_imputed, and its effect on the realised CCF of the affected pools is assessed in section 6.2 (DD-CCF-02). Target values are not imputed: 146 events without a balance at the default date were investigated with Collections, 131 were corrected at source from the daily balance history and 15 were excluded as part of E3. Outliers are identified with the documented criterion |realised CCF| > 10; the 1,288 events with realised CCFs above 1,000% are explained by very small undrawn amounts at the reference date, were verified against balance histories and are kept uncapped, because the pool design (MDD section 4.4) isolates facilities with high utilisation. Negative realised CCFs (balance reductions between reference date and default, 18.2% of events) are retained unchanged in the RDS; non-negativity is enforced only on the final pool estimates.

sections.heading: Representativeness – risk-driver distributions
sections.text: The RDS is compared with the application portfolio at 31 December 2025 (1,573,200 facilities with committed limit) using the PSI on each risk driver and on the pool distribution, with detailed tables in RDS Annex B. PSI values are 0.07 for utilisation band, 0.03 for delinquency status at reference date, 0.05 for limit size band and 0.11 for product type; the amber value for product type is explained by the growth of the overdraft share among defaulted facilities after the 2020 moratoria and does not affect the pool estimates, because product is itself a pooling criterion. The shares of missing and special values for the drivers are below 0.3% in both the RDS and the application portfolio. The retail exposure class assignment of all facilities in scope is verified: all obligors are natural persons, all facilities are revolving, unsecured and unconditionally cancellable, and the Bank's total exposure to each obligor in the retail revolving scope does not exceed EUR 100,000, which is monitored monthly in the exposure class assignment routine.

sections.heading: Representativeness – realised CCF levels, lending standards and limit management
sections.text: Representativeness is also assessed on the level of the target: the average realised CCF of the last three default years (2023–2025) is 66.1% for credit cards and 57.3% for overdrafts, against 66.8% and 57.0% for the full window, and a two-sample t-test per pool finds no significant difference at the 5% level. Lending standards changed twice in the window: the credit card limit policy of 2016 reduced maximum initial limits from EUR 7,500 to EUR 5,000, and in 2023 customers were given the option of instant limit increases in the mobile app. The account monitoring practice also changed: since 2019 limits of card accounts with a behavioural PD grade of R10 or worse are automatically reduced to the drawn amount plus EUR 250, and overdraft limits are blocked at 60 days past due; the effect of these practices on realised CCFs is analysed in MDD section 4.4 and the 2023 app functionality is covered by MoC category B (B-01). The Bank can monitor outstanding balances against committed lines on a daily basis for both products, and changes in outstandings per obligor and grade are reported monthly in the Retail Credit Risk Report.

sections.heading: Impact of exclusions
sections.text: The effect of each exclusion on the average realised CCF was quantified by recalculating the default-weighted average with and without the excluded events: E1 changes the credit card average by −0.1 and the overdraft average by −0.2 percentage points, E2 by +0.0 and −0.4, and E3 by −0.1 for overdrafts. The aggregate effect of all exclusions on the long-run average CCF is −0.1 percentage points for credit cards and −0.6 percentage points for overdrafts before pooling; within the pools the largest effect is +0.3 percentage points (OD-1). The distribution of utilisation bands and delinquency status is unchanged by the exclusions (PSI < 0.01), so the exclusions do not reduce the representativeness of the RDS for the application portfolio. The analysis code is part of the tagged build (script analysis/exclusion_impact.py).

sections.heading: Data quality assessment
sections.text: The data quality assessment of the RDS was performed in May–June 2026 under MRM-STD-022 against the dimensions completeness, accuracy, consistency, timeliness, validity and uniqueness, with results per critical data element reported in the data quality assessment EVD-03-DQ and summarised here. All critical data elements are within the green thresholds except the overdraft limit at reference date in 2012–2014 (completeness 97.9% before imputation, amber) and the card balance history for March–April 2017 (two monthly snapshots missing in the original delivery, red before reload). The RDS reconciles to the finance ledger: drawn balances of the in-scope portfolio per year-end snapshot differ by at most 0.08% from the ledger, and record counts per reference date match the source extracts exactly.

sections.heading: Data deficiencies
sections.text: The data deficiency log records each deficiency with identifier, affected period, variables and segments, DQ dimension, cause, impact, treatment, owner and target date; each open deficiency is cross-referenced to the MDD limitations log and to its margin of conservatism category. DD-CCF-01 – default flag approximated for 2012–2015 (all segments; accuracy/consistency): impact −0.3 percentage points on realised CCFs; treatment MoC category A (A-01); permanent, reassessed annually; limitation L-01. DD-CCF-02 – overdraft limit history not migrated from CBS-L for 2,904 events in 2012–2014 (overdraft pools; completeness): limit imputed from product parameters; impact estimated at ±1.2 percentage points on the affected pools; treatment MoC category A (A-02); owner Head of Daily Banking Data, remediation not feasible at source; limitation L-02. DD-CCF-03 – undefined realised CCF for 1,954 over-limit facilities at the reference date (pools CC-4 and OD-4; appropriateness): treatment MoC category A (A-03); limitation L-03. DD-CCF-04 – two monthly card snapshots missing in the 2017 processor migration (credit cards; completeness): remediated at source by a reload from the processor archive in April 2026 and closed after re-running the DQ checks; no MoC. All deficiencies affecting critical data elements are also recorded in the Bank data issue register (DIR-2026-0412 to DIR-2026-0415) with owner and target date. None of the deficiencies is rated high or critical, so no escalation to the Group Data Governance Committee was required.

sections.heading: Personal data – purpose, lawful basis and minimisation
sections.text: The RDS contains personal data of natural persons: pseudonymised customer and account keys, product, limit, balance and transaction aggregates, delinquency and default status, account open date and postcode region (first two digits). The purposes of processing are the development, validation and application of IRB conversion factors for own funds requirements and, as a secondary use, IFRS 9 impairment; these purposes are recorded in the Record of Processing under entry ROP-CRM-0147, to which the model inventory record of MDL-03 refers. The lawful basis is Article 6(1)(c) GDPR (legal obligation under CRR Articles 143 and 179) for development and application, recorded before processing started; the reuse of account data collected for contract performance was assessed as compatible under Article 6(4) GDPR in compatibility assessment CA-2025-031, considering the link between purposes, the context of collection, the nature of the data, the consequences for data subjects and the pseudonymisation applied. Legitimate interests are not relied upon, so no legitimate interest assessment is required. Each personal data attribute is justified by its relevance to CCF estimation in RDS Annex A; the customer name, address, date of birth, income and transaction descriptions are not extracted, and the postcode is kept at two-digit level only for representativeness analysis. No special categories of personal data under Article 9 GDPR are processed; transaction descriptions, which could reveal health or religious information, are excluded at extraction.

sections.heading: Personal data – DPIA and data protection by design
sections.text: A DPIA (DPIA-2026-061) was completed on 3 February 2026 before the extraction for the RDS started; it contains a systematic description of the processing and purposes, an assessment of necessity and proportionality, an assessment of the risks to data subjects and the measures envisaged. The Data Protection Officer advised on 27 January 2026 that the residual risk is low; prior consultation of the Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens was therefore not required. The DPIA will be reviewed on every material change of the model, including new personal data attributes, and at the latest in February 2029. Data protection by design is implemented in the pipeline: direct identifiers are replaced by keyed tokens at extraction, the key is held by the Bank's pseudonymisation service operated by Group Data Management, and the development environment has no access to the key. No re-identification of the development data has taken place; any re-identification requires a Privacy Office-approved purpose and is logged by the pseudonymisation service. No personal data are transferred outside the EEA; the card processor processes the data in the Netherlands and Germany.

sections.text: The RDS is held only in the approved secure analytics environment SAE-Risk with role-based access limited to eleven named users in Retail Credit Risk Modelling and Model Validation; test environments use the pseudonymised RDS only. sections.heading: Fair treatment – protected attributes and proxy screening
sections.text: Protected attributes (gender, age, nationality, ethnic origin, religion) are not included in the RDS and are not candidate drivers of the model; age is not used. Proxy screening was performed on all candidate drivers: the association of each candidate with age band and gender, obtained through a separate privacy-approved extract, is below a Cramér's V of 0.10, except for account tenure (V = 0.19 with age band), which was not retained as a driver. The postcode region is used only for representativeness analysis and not as a driver. The CCF is applied to exposures and does not score natural persons for credit decisions; the results of proxy screening are documented here and in MDD section 4.3.

sections.heading: Reproducibility
sections.text: The RDS is built entirely by versioned code in the Bank's GitLab repository crm-retail/ccf-rev, tag rds-v3.0.0 (commit 8c41e2d), from the source snapshots with reference date 31 March 2026 (CardServ archive, Core24, CollectPlus, DefaultHub and ledger extracts). A full rebuild from the source snapshots on 11 June 2026 reproduced the frozen RDS exactly: 282,412,655 account-month records and 133,211 default events, with identical checksums of the event table. The frozen RDS RDS-CCF-REV-3.0 is stored read-only in the model data store (MDS/CRM/RDS/CCF-REV/3.0), protected against alteration, and is referenced by this identifier in the MDD; any correction will be made in a new RDS version with the original retained. The build code, lineage, metadata and software environment (Python 3.11.8, pandas 2.2.1, pyspark 3.5.0, recorded in environment.lock) are archived with the RDS so that the development data can be reproduced for the life of the model and at least ten years after decommissioning. The build code was reviewed by a second developer who did not write it (review record in merge request !412) before the RDS was frozen.

sections.heading: Purpose and scope
sections.text: This document describes the reference data set (RDS) RDS-CCF-REV-3.0 used to develop and calibrate the conversion factor model CCF-REV v3.0 (inventory identifier MDL-03) for the Bank's retail revolving exposures: credit cards and arranged current account overdrafts granted to natural persons in the Netherlands. The model estimates the conversion factor (CCF) applied to the undrawn part of committed revolving limits in the calculation of exposure values under the Advanced IRB approach, in accordance with CRR Articles 166(8a) to 166(8c) and 182. The rating system is used within the Bank's IRB permission for the retail exposure class (qualifying revolving retail and other retail exposures), which has been approved since 2008; the experience test of CRR Article 145 is therefore met for the range of application of this rating system. The document follows the RDS documentation template of MRM-STD-021 Annex A, is stored in the controlled document repository linked to the model inventory (DocHub folder MDL-03/RDS) and is subject to version control with a document history in section 9. Visser (Retail Credit Risk Modelling, not involved in the RDS build); approver M. de Vries, Model Owner and Director Retail Credit Risk; approval date 19 June 2026.

sections.heading: Observation period
sections.text: The RDS covers all default events with a default date between 1 January 2012 and 31 December 2025 on credit card and overdraft facilities, each linked to the monthly account snapshot at the reference date twelve months before default; the underlying account panel therefore starts on 1 January 2011. The base panel contains 282.4 million account-month records for 1,934,700 unique facilities of 1,512,300 unique obligors, and the frozen RDS contains 133,211 default events (56,480 credit card and 76,731 overdraft events). With fourteen years of default dates, the observation period exceeds the minimum of five years required for retail conversion factors by CRR Article 182(3) and CRM-STD-100 §6.2. Snapshots are taken at each month-end from the Retail Data Warehouse (RDW); the default events are sourced from the Bank's default register and are available with a daily default date.

sections.heading: Choice of observation window
sections.text: The window starts in January 2012 because complete monthly limit and balance histories for credit cards are available from January 2011 onwards, which is the earliest possible reference date for a twelve-month fixed horizon; earlier card data were held by the previous processor and were not migrated at transaction level. The window covers the Dutch recession of 2012–2013 with the unemployment peak of early 2014, the benign years 2015–2019, the COVID-19 period 2020–2021 with extensive government support and the inflation shock of 2022–2023, and therefore contains a mix of economic conditions relevant for current and foreseeable conditions. Two system migrations fall in the window: the migration of current accounts from the legacy core banking system CBS-L to Core24 in October 2014 and the change of card processor in March 2017; both are treated in section 6.2 (deficiencies DD-CCF-02 and DD-CCF-04). The identification of the economic downturn relevant for conversion factors and its coverage by the window are documented in the downturn report EVD-03-DT and summarised in MDD chapter 5. All defaults from the window are used; no sub-period is excluded, so that the long-run average reflects all observed defaults in the data sources.

sections.heading: Target variable and outcome horizon
sections.text: The target variable is the realised conversion factor of each defaulted facility, calculated with a fixed horizon of twelve months: CCF = (EAD at default − drawn amount at reference date) / (limit at reference date − drawn amount at reference date), where the reference date is the month-end snapshot twelve months before the default date. The EAD at default is the outstanding balance on the default date including capitalised interest and fees; drawings, interest and fees after the default date are not part of the realised CCF and are captured in the realised LGD of the retail revolving LGD model (MDL-04), in line with CRM-STD-100 §10.2. Realised CCFs are not capped at 100%, and the EAD at default is not capped at the limit or at the principal amount outstanding, so that over-limit drawings, capitalised interest and fees are fully reflected in the RDS. Where a facility was opened less than twelve months before default, the snapshot at the end of the month of origination is used as reference date; this applies to 3,912 events (2.9%) and is recorded in the RDS field ref_date_type. Facilities whose drawn amount equalled or exceeded the limit at the reference date (undrawn amount ≤ 0) have an undefined realised CCF; the 1,954 events concerned are kept in the RDS with their realised additional drawings but are not used in the average realised CCF (see DD-CCF-03).

sections.heading: Default definition – days past due and materiality threshold
sections.text: An obligor is in default when it is more than 90 days past due on a material credit obligation or is considered unlikely to pay; any amount of principal, interest or fee not paid on its due date is recognised as past due. The materiality threshold is the one set by the ECB for all significant institutions under Delegated Regulation (EU) 2018/171: EUR 100 absolute and 1% relative for retail exposures. The absolute component is compared with the sum of all amounts past due owed by the obligor to the Bank and its subsidiaries, and the relative component divides that sum by the obligor's total on-balance-sheet exposure excluding equity exposures. The days-past-due counter starts on the first day on which both components are exceeded and restarts when either component is no longer exceeded; default under the past due criterion occurs on the 91st consecutive day, and no months-in-arrears proxy is used. Where a repayment schedule is modified, days past due are counted on the modified schedule, and payment holidays granted under contractual rights or by law (including the COVID-19 moratoria of 2020) were not counted as past due but were screened for unlikeliness to pay. Counting is suspended for disputed amounts only when the dispute is before a court or the Dutch financial services complaints institute Kifid; 212 such cases are flagged in the RDS. All thresholds are denominated in euro and all exposures in scope are euro-denominated, so the currency provision of Article 5 of the RTS does not apply.

sections.heading: Default definition – level of application and date of default
sections.text: Default is applied at obligor level for all retail exposures in line with the Bank's risk management practice (CR-STD-110 §4.2): when an obligor defaults, all its credit obligations, including cards and overdrafts not in arrears, are flagged as defaulted in all systems. The option to apply the definition at facility level for retail exposures is not used, so no facility-level threshold is applied and the facility-level threshold test does not arise. Because the definition is applied at obligor level, the materiality threshold is calculated at obligor level, and a joint obligor (for example a joint current account of two partners) is treated as a separate obligor in the threshold calculation; the default of a joint obligation leads to default of the individual exposures of both co-obligors unless the exceptions of paragraph 97 of EBA/GL/2016/07 apply. The date of default is the first day on which any default criterion is met; dpd counters are calculated daily in the collections system CollectPlus, so the date of default equals the date the past due criterion was actually fulfilled. Default identification is consistent across the card processor feed, Core24 and the mortgage and consumer loan systems through the Group customer identifier, so a default of the obligor on any product is flagged on the credit card and overdraft facilities without undue delay. There are no legal impediments to data exchange between the Bank and its consumer credit subsidiary, so the inconsistency described in paragraph 81 of EBA/GL/2016/07 does not arise.

sections.heading: Default definition – probation periods and multiple defaults
sections.text: An obligor returns to non-default status only when no default trigger has applied for at least three months and the assessment of its behaviour and financial situation shows that the improvement is factual and permanent; after a distressed restructuring the probation period is at least twelve months and requires a material payment, no amount past due and no concerns about full repayment. The probation start date and status are stored for every default event in the fields prob_start_dt and prob_status. Where an obligor defaults again within twelve months of returning to non-default status, both events are merged into one default event starting on the first default date; 5,218 facility events were merged in this way and the merged events keep the reference date of the first default. Re-default rates are analysed annually by default trigger: of the obligors cured in 2022–2024, 8.7% re-defaulted within twelve months (forbearance-related cures: 17.4%), which the Credit Risk Management annual review of 2025 judged acceptable without extending the probation period. For 2012–2015 probation periods could not be reconstructed because cure dates are not available in the legacy data; for these years the return to non-default was approximated by three consecutive months without arrears, as stated in section 3.3.4.

sections.heading: Historical approximation of the default flag
sections.text: The RDS distinguishes three default-definition periods, identified by the field dod_regime: P1 (January 2012 – December 2015), in which the flag is approximated; P2 (January 2016 – November 2020), in which the production flag is available but used an internal absolute threshold of EUR 50 without relative component; and P3 (from December 2020), in which the current definition with the regulatory threshold applies. For P1 the past due criterion was reconstructed from daily arrears amounts in CollectPlus, applying the EUR 100 / 1% threshold retrospectively; unlikeliness to pay was approximated from bankruptcy (WSNP debt restructuring) registrations, forbearance flags and write-offs, while non-accrued status was not available. For P2 the past due flag was re-derived from the daily arrears data with the regulatory threshold, which removed 1.8% of P2 default events that were caused by amounts between EUR 50 and EUR 100. The production default flag and the RDS flag constructed by the build code were reconciled for P3: 99.6% of default events agree on obligor and date within one day, and all 318 differences were explained by retroactive corrections in the default register. The effect of the approximation was quantified by comparing realised CCFs of P1 with a P3-based benchmark: the approximated flag advances the default date by 11 days on average, which lowers realised CCFs by 0.3 percentage points; the deficiency is logged as DD-CCF-01 and linked to MoC category A (A-01).

sections.heading: Unlikeliness-to-pay triggers – automatic triggers
sections.text: The following UTP triggers lead to default automatically: non-accrued status; specific credit risk adjustment or IFRS 9 Stage 3 classification; sale of a credit obligation at a credit-related economic loss above 5%; distressed restructuring with a diminished financial obligation above 1%; bankruptcy or admission to the statutory debt restructuring scheme (WSNP); and charge-off of the account. Specific credit risk adjustments are UTP indications only where they result from a significant perceived decline in credit quality; the collective allowances for Stage 1 and Stage 2 are not treated as UTP. The diminished financial obligation is calculated as (NPV0 − NPV1)/NPV0 with cash flows discounted at the original effective interest rate; forborne facilities below the 1% threshold are assessed for other UTP indications such as repeated forbearance or a large final instalment, and all forborne non-performing exposures are classified as defaulted. Charged-off unsecured retail claims are periodically sold to debt purchasers after default; the loss on sale L = (E − P)/E is calculated per sale, sales above the 5% threshold are recorded as defaults at the moment of sale where default had not been recognised before, and the reasons for each sale are documented by Collections. Automatic triggers are evaluated daily, and a monthly control compares the forborne non-performing list with the default register to verify that all such exposures are flagged as defaulted.

sections.heading: Unlikeliness-to-pay triggers – case-by-case indicators
sections.text: Additional UTP indicators for retail revolving exposures (fraud by the customer, significant loss of income reported to Collections, multiple forbearance within 24 months, BKR negative registration at another lender) lead to a case-by-case assessment by the Collections expert team, completed within 30 days of detection and recorded with its rationale. For each indicator the identification method, information source and monitoring frequency are defined in the UTP operating procedure (Collections procedure COL-P-014 v5), which maps each trigger to source-system fields and assigns responsibilities. Technical past due situations are recognised only for Bank data or system errors, payment execution failures and payment allocation time lags; they are documented and corrected within 30 days, and the 2,114 technical past due events identified in the default register are removed from the RDS. Because UTP labels are set partly by human judgement, the labelling guideline of COL-P-014 is applied by the central Collections team only, and a semi-annual analysis compares UTP rates per assessor; the 2025 analysis found no systematic differences between assessors (chi-square p = 0.41). Contagion between connected retail obligors is limited to joint credit obligations as described in section 3.3.2; no further group-of-connected-clients contagion applies to natural persons in scope.

sections.heading: Data sources
sections.text: The RDS is built from five source systems: the card processor files delivered monthly by CardServ B.V. (card limits, balances, transactions), the current account system Core24 and its predecessor CBS-L (overdraft limits and balances), the collections system CollectPlus (daily arrears and dpd counters), the default register DefaultHub maintained under CR-STD-110, and the finance ledger (write-offs and reconciliation totals). Each source belongs to a data domain with exactly one Data Owner recorded in the Group Data Catalogue: Cards (Head of Retail Cards), Payments and Accounts (Head of Daily Banking), Collections (Head of Retail Collections), Credit Risk Data (Director Credit Risk Management) and Finance Data (Head of Financial Reporting). The authoritative source for every data type is defined: CardServ for card balances and limits, Core24 for overdraft balances and limits, DefaultHub for default status and dates, and the finance ledger for write-offs. Card processing is performed by the third party CardServ B.V. under an outsourcing agreement; the Bank retains full responsibility for the data, receives the complete monthly account file, reconciles it with the ledger and has contractual access rights to transaction-level data, and the third-party involvement is recorded in the outsourcing register (OR-2017-022). No external or pooled data are used in the RDS; the provisions on external data, pooled data and the adjustment of external default definitions are therefore not applicable.

sections.heading: Lineage and critical data elements
sections.text: Lineage from the source systems to the RDS is documented for every variable in RDS Annex A, identifying the source table and field, each intermediate store (RDW staging, RDW core, model data store), every transformation, filter, join and aggregation with a reference to the build script and line range, and the extraction frequency and timing. Discarded variables that were used to construct retained variables, such as the daily balance history used to derive the maximum balance before default, are included in the lineage. For the card processor data the lineage starts at the point of receipt in the Bank's secure file gateway and records the provider, the data product (monthly account master file ACCMAST) and the delivery date of each file. All model input variables and all data elements used to construct the target variable (limit and drawn amount at the reference date, balance at default, default flag and default date) are designated critical data elements, each with a business definition, a technical definition and DQ rules per applicable dimension. The lineage was updated in March 2026 to reflect the replacement of the RDW staging layer, before the changed data were used in development, and the Data Owners confirmed that no change to definitions or transformation logic of these elements is planned without prior notice to the Model Owner. Aggregation is fully automated; the only manual interventions in the data flow are the expert mapping of 43 legacy CBS-L product codes to current products and the list of disputed accounts, both held as version-controlled input files and identified explicitly in the lineage with their four-eyes control.

sections.heading: Exclusions
sections.text: Exclusions are applied in the following order, each with a documented reason approved by the Model Owner on 12 June 2026 (approval record in ticket CRMRET-2214). E1 – technical past due events: 2,114 events (1.5% of the 141,164 events after merging multiple defaults; 1,037 credit card, 1,077 overdraft), removed because they are not defaults. E2 – facilities without a committed limit at the reference date (tolerated, unarranged overdrafts and cancelled card limits): 4,806 events (3.4%; 4,211 overdraft, 595 credit card), removed because no undrawn commitment exists to which a CCF can be applied; their exposure value equals the drawn amount. E3 – duplicate facility records created by the Core24 migration in October 2014: 1,033 events (0.7%, all overdraft), removed after matching legacy and new account numbers. In the overdraft segment the exclusions sum to 6.1% of events, which exceeds the 5% threshold of MRM-STD-022 §5.3; the exclusions were therefore approved by the Model Owner and reported to Model Validation on 12 June 2026. For each exclusion the conclusion of the impact analysis is stated in section 5.3: none of the exclusions changes the average realised CCF of any segment by more than 0.4 percentage points.

sections.heading: Missing values and outliers
sections.text: The treatment of missing values is documented per variable in RDS Annex C, distinguishing values missing at random, missing for a structural reason (for example no previous limit change for new accounts) and missing because of a data deficiency. The only imputation concerns the overdraft limit at the reference date for 2,904 overdraft events in 2012–2014 whose limit history was not migrated from CBS-L; the limit is reconstructed from the product parameter table and the customer's limit at migration, is flagged in the field lim_imputed, and its effect on the realised CCF of the affected pools is assessed in section 6.2 (DD-CCF-02). Target values are not imputed: 146 events without a balance at the default date were investigated with Collections, 131 were corrected at source from the daily balance history and 15 were excluded as part of E3. Outliers are identified with the documented criterion |realised CCF| > 10; the 1,288 events with realised CCFs above 1,000% are explained by very small undrawn amounts at the reference date, were verified against balance histories and are kept uncapped, because the pool design (MDD section 4.4) isolates facilities with high utilisation. Negative realised CCFs (balance reductions between reference date and default, 18.2% of events) are retained unchanged in the RDS; non-negativity is enforced only on the final pool estimates.

sections.heading: Representativeness – risk-driver distributions
sections.text: The RDS is compared with the application portfolio at 31 December 2025 (1,573,200 facilities with committed limit) using the PSI on each risk driver and on the pool distribution, with detailed tables in RDS Annex B. PSI values are 0.07 for utilisation band, 0.03 for delinquency status at reference date, 0.05 for limit size band and 0.11 for product type; the amber value for product type is explained by the growth of the overdraft share among defaulted facilities after the 2020 moratoria and does not affect the pool estimates, because product is itself a pooling criterion. The shares of missing and special values for the drivers are below 0.3% in both the RDS and the application portfolio. The retail exposure class assignment of all facilities in scope is verified: all obligors are natural persons, all facilities are revolving, unsecured and unconditionally cancellable, and the Bank's total exposure to each obligor in the retail revolving scope does not exceed EUR 100,000, which is monitored monthly in the exposure class assignment routine.

sections.heading: Representativeness – realised CCF levels, lending standards and limit management
sections.text: Representativeness is also assessed on the level of the target: the average realised CCF of the last three default years (2023–2025) is 66.1% for credit cards and 57.3% for overdrafts, against 66.8% and 57.0% for the full window, and a two-sample t-test per pool finds no significant difference at the 5% level. Lending standards changed twice in the window: the credit card limit policy of 2016 reduced maximum initial limits from EUR 7,500 to EUR 5,000, and in 2023 customers were given the option of instant limit increases in the mobile app. The account monitoring practice also changed: since 2019 limits of card accounts with a behavioural PD grade of R10 or worse are automatically reduced to the drawn amount plus EUR 250, and overdraft limits are blocked at 60 days past due; the effect of these practices on realised CCFs is analysed in MDD section 4.4 and the 2023 app functionality is covered by MoC category B (B-01). The Bank can monitor outstanding balances against committed lines on a daily basis for both products, and changes in outstandings per obligor and grade are reported monthly in the Retail Credit Risk Report.

sections.heading: Impact of exclusions
sections.text: The effect of each exclusion on the average realised CCF was quantified by recalculating the default-weighted average with and without the excluded events: E1 changes the credit card average by −0.1 and the overdraft average by −0.2 percentage points, E2 by +0.0 and −0.4, and E3 by −0.1 for overdrafts. The aggregate effect of all exclusions on the long-run average CCF is −0.1 percentage points for credit cards and −0.6 percentage points for overdrafts before pooling; within the pools the largest effect is +0.3 percentage points (OD-1). The distribution of utilisation bands and delinquency status is unchanged by the exclusions (PSI < 0.01), so the exclusions do not reduce the representativeness of the RDS for the application portfolio. The analysis code is part of the tagged build (script analysis/exclusion_impact.py).

sections.heading: Data quality assessment
sections.text: The data quality assessment of the RDS was performed in May–June 2026 under MRM-STD-022 against the dimensions completeness, accuracy, consistency, timeliness, validity and uniqueness, with results per critical data element reported in the data quality assessment EVD-03-DQ and summarised here. All critical data elements are within the green thresholds except the overdraft limit at reference date in 2012–2014 (completeness 97.9% before imputation, amber) and the card balance history for March–April 2017 (two monthly snapshots missing in the original delivery, red before reload). The RDS reconciles to the finance ledger: drawn balances of the in-scope portfolio per year-end snapshot differ by at most 0.08% from the ledger, and record counts per reference date match the source extracts exactly. The DQ assessment concludes that the RDS is fit for the development and calibration of CCF-REV v3.0, subject to the deficiencies listed in section 6.2, and was signed off by the model developer and the Model Owner on 15 June 2026, before the RDS was frozen.

sections.heading: Data deficiencies
sections.text: The data deficiency log records each deficiency with identifier, affected period, variables and segments, DQ dimension, cause, impact, treatment, owner and target date; each open deficiency is cross-referenced to the MDD limitations log and to its margin of conservatism category. DD-CCF-01 – default flag approximated for 2012–2015 (all segments; accuracy/consistency): impact −0.3 percentage points on realised CCFs; treatment MoC category A (A-01); permanent, reassessed annually; limitation L-01. DD-CCF-02 – overdraft limit history not migrated from CBS-L for 2,904 events in 2012–2014 (overdraft pools; completeness): limit imputed from product parameters; impact estimated at ±1.2 percentage points on the affected pools; treatment MoC category A (A-02); owner Head of Daily Banking Data, remediation not feasible at source; limitation L-02. DD-CCF-03 – undefined realised CCF for 1,954 over-limit facilities at the reference date (pools CC-4 and OD-4; appropriateness): treatment MoC category A (A-03); limitation L-03. DD-CCF-04 – two monthly card snapshots missing in the 2017 processor migration (credit cards; completeness): remediated at source by a reload from the processor archive in April 2026 and closed after re-running the DQ checks; no MoC. All deficiencies affecting critical data elements are also recorded in the Bank data issue register (DIR-2026-0412 to DIR-2026-0415) with owner and target date. None of the deficiencies is rated high or critical, so no escalation to the Group Data Governance Committee was required.

sections.heading: Personal data – purpose, lawful basis and minimisation
sections.text: The RDS contains personal data of natural persons: pseudonymised customer and account keys, product, limit, balance and transaction aggregates, delinquency and default status, account open date and postcode region (first two digits). The purposes of processing are the development, validation and application of IRB conversion factors for own funds requirements and, as a secondary use, IFRS 9 impairment; these purposes are recorded in the Record of Processing under entry ROP-CRM-0147, to which the model inventory record of MDL-03 refers. The lawful basis is Article 6(1)(c) GDPR (legal obligation under CRR Articles 143 and 179) for development and application, recorded before processing started; the reuse of account data collected for contract performance was assessed as compatible under Article 6(4) GDPR in compatibility assessment CA-2025-031, considering the link between purposes, the context of collection, the nature of the data, the consequences for data subjects and the pseudonymisation applied. Legitimate interests are not relied upon, so no legitimate interest assessment is required. Each personal data attribute is justified by its relevance to CCF estimation in RDS Annex A; the customer name, address, date of birth, income and transaction descriptions are not extracted, and the postcode is kept at two-digit level only for representativeness analysis. No special categories of personal data under Article 9 GDPR are processed; transaction descriptions, which could reveal health or religious information, are excluded at extraction.

sections.heading: Personal data – DPIA and data protection by design
sections.text: A DPIA (DPIA-2026-061) was completed on 3 February 2026 before the extraction for the RDS started; it contains a systematic description of the processing and purposes, an assessment of necessity and proportionality, an assessment of the risks to data subjects and the measures envisaged. The Data Protection Officer advised on 27 January 2026 that the residual risk is low; prior consultation of the Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens was therefore not required. The DPIA will be reviewed on every material change of the model, including new personal data attributes, and at the latest in February 2029. Data protection by design is implemented in the pipeline: direct identifiers are replaced by keyed tokens at extraction, the key is held by the Bank's pseudonymisation service operated by Group Data Management, and the development environment has no access to the key. No re-identification of the development data has taken place; any re-identification requires a Privacy Office-approved purpose and is logged by the pseudonymisation service. No personal data are transferred outside the EEA; the card processor processes the data in the Netherlands and Germany.

sections.heading: Personal data – security, accuracy and retention
sections.text: The RDS is held only in the approved secure analytics environment SAE-Risk with role-based access limited to eleven named users in Retail Credit Risk Modelling and Model Validation; test environments use the pseudonymised RDS only. Accuracy of the personal data is ensured by the reconciliations in section 6.1, and corrections of source data are made in the source systems and flow into the next RDS version rather than being changed in the frozen RDS. Retention: the frozen RDS is retained for the period of use of the model and ten years after decommissioning, as required by DATA-POL-001 §10.2 and CRR Article 176; the Privacy Office approved this longer retention on 10 February 2026 (PO-2026-044), after which the data are deleted or irreversibly anonymised and deletion is evidenced in the retention register. The Model Owner is accountable for demonstrating compliance with the GDPR principles for this processing, supported by the DPIA, the Record of Processing entry and this chapter.

sections.heading: Fair treatment – protected attributes and proxy screening
sections.text: Protected attributes (gender, age, nationality, ethnic origin, religion) are not included in the RDS and are not candidate drivers of the model; age is not used. Proxy screening was performed on all candidate drivers: the association of each candidate with age band and gender, obtained through a separate privacy-approved extract, is below a Cramér's V of 0.10, except for account tenure (V = 0.19 with age band), which was not retained as a driver. The postcode region is used only for representativeness analysis and not as a driver. The CCF is applied to exposures and does not score natural persons for credit decisions; the results of proxy screening are documented here and in MDD section 4.3.

sections.heading: Reproducibility
sections.text: The RDS is built entirely by versioned code in the Bank's GitLab repository crm-retail/ccf-rev, tag rds-v3.0.0 (commit 8c41e2d), from the source snapshots with reference date 31 March 2026 (CardServ archive, Core24, CollectPlus, DefaultHub and ledger extracts). A full rebuild from the source snapshots on 11 June 2026 reproduced the frozen RDS exactly: 282,412,655 account-month records and 133,211 default events, with identical checksums of the event table. The frozen RDS RDS-CCF-REV-3.0 is stored read-only in the model data store (MDS/CRM/RDS/CCF-REV/3.0), protected against alteration, and is referenced by this identifier in the MDD; any correction will be made in a new RDS version with the original retained. The build code, lineage, metadata and software environment (Python 3.11.8, pandas 2.2.1, pyspark 3.5.0, recorded in environment.lock) are archived with the RDS so that the development data can be reproduced for the life of the model and at least ten years after decommissioning. The build code was reviewed by a second developer who did not write it (review record in merge request !412) before the RDS was frozen.

sections.heading: Purpose and intended use
sections.text: CCF-REV v3.0 estimates the conversion factors applied to the undrawn committed limits of retail credit cards and arranged current account overdrafts of natural persons, for the calculation of exposure values under the Advanced IRB approach (CRR Article 166(8a) to (8c) and Article 182). Version 3.0 replaces CCF-REV v2.1, which used a cohort approach with annual cohorts on 1 January; the cohort approach does not meet the twelve-month fixed-horizon requirement of CRR Article 182(1)(g), applicable since 1 January 2025 under Regulation (EU) 2024/1623, and the redevelopment implements that requirement. Secondary uses are the IFRS 9 lifetime EAD of the same portfolios (without MoC and downturn adjustment), the ICAAP economic capital model and the credit risk stress test. Users are Capital Management (own funds calculation), Retail Credit Risk Management (limit policy and risk appetite), Retail Pricing (risk-adjusted pricing of card products), Finance – Impairments and Enterprise Risk Management (ICAAP and stress testing). Cover block: title MDD CCF Retail Revolving; model CCF-REV v3.0 (MDL-03); document version 0.9; status draft for review; author S. Bakker; reviewer R. Jansen; approvers M. de Vries (Model Owner) and E. Smit (Head of Retail Credit Risk Modelling); not yet approved.

Version 3.0 replaces CCF-REV v2.1, which used a cohort approach with annual cohorts on 1 January; the cohort approach does not meet the twelve-month fixed-horizon requirement of CRR Article 182(1)(g), applicable since 1 January 2025 under Regulation (EU) 2024/1623, and the redevelopment implements that requirement.

sections.heading: Range of application and exposure class
sections.text: The range of application comprises all credit card facilities (468,300 accounts, committed limits EUR 1,392 million, drawn EUR 341 million at 31 December 2026) and all current accounts with an arranged overdraft limit (1,104,900 accounts, limits EUR 1,268 million, drawn EUR 152 million) of natural persons booked by the Bank in the Netherlands. All facilities are revolving, unconditionally cancellable commitments that attract a 10% conversion factor under the Standardised Approach (CRR Article 111), so they are not subject to a 100% SA conversion factor and own estimates of conversion factors are permitted under CRR Article 166(8b). Exposures to institutions, financial sector entities and large corporates are outside the range of application, so the restriction of CRR Article 147a(1) on own CCF estimates for these exposures is respected by construction. The facilities are assigned to the retail exposure class by the exposure class assignment routine, which applies the CRR Article 147(5) and 154(4) criteria (natural persons, revolving, unsecured, total exposure to the obligor up to EUR 100,000, managed on a pooled basis) in a fixed sequence that has not changed since 2019. The IRB approach is applied to all retail exposures of the Bank; the credit card portfolio of the Belgian branch (3,100 accounts, EUR 11.8 million limits) is under permanent partial use of the Standardised Approach under CRR Article 150(1), approved by the ECB as immaterial in size and risk profile, and its share (0.4% of retail revolving limits) is monitored quarterly against the triggers of the roll-out plan (maximum 1% of the retail EAD). The roll-out plan agreed with the ECB has been completed for the retail exposure class, and no exposures are held back from the IRB approach to reduce own funds requirements.

sections.heading: Use of model outputs and internal parameters
sections.text: The CCF estimates play an essential role beyond own funds: the resulting EAD enters the internal capital allocation to the Retail Cards and Daily Banking business lines, the credit risk appetite metrics (expected loss and RWA density of retail unsecured lending), risk-adjusted pricing of card products, the calibration of limit policies (maximum initial limits and limit-increase rules) and the quarterly management reporting to the Retail Credit Committee. For IFRS 9 the Bank uses the same pools and realised CCFs but removes the MoC and the downturn add-on and applies a point-in-time adjustment; for pricing, the downturn add-on is also removed; these differences are documented and justified in the parameter mapping table PMT-CCF-2027 and the internal parameters are derived from the IRB parameters. The CCF is not used for decisions on individual customers: limit increase and approval decisions are based on the behavioural PD, policy rules and affordability, so the model does not produce automated individual decisions within the meaning of Article 22 GDPR. All risk parameters used for the risk appetite metrics of the retail unsecured portfolio are produced by models registered in the model inventory and approved under MRM-POL-001.

sections.heading: Model structure and components
sections.text: The rating system for conversion factors consists of four clearly separated components: (a) the assignment of each facility to one of ten CCF pools at the monthly reference date; (b) the long-run average (LRA) realised CCF per pool; (c) the downturn add-on per pool; and (d) the margin of conservatism per pool, followed by the application of the exposure value floor of CRR Article 166(8c) at facility level. The pools are defined by product (credit card, overdraft), utilisation band at the reference date and delinquency status at the reference date, as specified in section 4.4. The model is a statistical model developed in-house by Retail Credit Risk Modelling; no vendor model or proprietary third-party technology is used, and the external card processor provides data only. A third party can replicate the pool assignment from sections 4.4 and 5.3 and the implementation specification IS-CCF-REV-3.0 without further information.

sections.heading: Dependencies on other models
sections.text: The model depends on the retail behavioural PD model (MDL-02) only for the pool definition of delinquency status, which uses the dpd counter directly and not the PD, and on the default register for the default flag; it provides the EAD to the retail revolving LGD model (MDL-04), whose realised LGD includes drawings after default. Changes to the default definition therefore affect this model and are assessed as changes to all IRB rating systems under MRM-STD-050 and Delegated Regulation (EU) No 529/2014, as required by CR-STD-110 §10.3. The model complexity was assessed as Low in the ECB complexity assessment performed by MRM on 2 December 2025 (no machine learning, no dynamic recalibration). The model framework is governed by the Bank's written Model Risk Management Policy MRM-POL-001, which defines what constitutes a model and the components of the model risk framework.

sections.heading: Use in stress testing
sections.text: In the ICAAP and in the EBA and internal credit risk stress tests, the CCF per pool is stressed with the sensitivity of the quarterly average realised CCF to the unemployment rate estimated in the downturn report (EVD-03-DT, +0.9 percentage points per percentage point of unemployment), applied to the severe but plausible recession scenarios of the Bank's stress-testing framework. In the 2026 ICAAP adverse scenario (unemployment +3.8 percentage points) the stressed CCF increases the retail revolving EAD by 4.1% and the RWEA of the rating system by EUR 19 million; the result is part of the ICAAP report approved by the Management Board on 24 March 2027. The stress test covers the full range of application of the rating system.

sections.heading: Reference data set
sections.text: The model is developed on the frozen RDS RDS-CCF-REV-3.0 described in the approved RDS documentation EVD-03-RDS version 1.0 of 19 June 2026: 133,211 default events with default dates between January 2012 and December 2025, each linked to its reference date twelve months before default. The RDS stores for every defaulted facility the pool assignment data at the reference date, the realised CCF and the default date, and the production system stores the estimated CCF per pool and the pool of each facility in the twelve months before default, as required by CRR Article 176(4). Data deficiencies DD-CCF-01 to DD-CCF-03 of the RDS documentation are carried into the limitations log (L-01 to L-03) and the MoC register (A-01 to A-03). The same default definition is used for the CCF, PD and LGD models of the retail revolving rating system, so the RDS is consistent with the default events used in MDL-02 and MDL-04.

sections.heading: Development, out-of-sample and out-of-time samples
sections.text: Before any estimation, the samples were defined in the development plan: the development sample consists of the default years 2012–2023 (112,406 events), of which a random 30% hold-out stratified by product and default year is the out-of-sample (33,722 events), and the out-of-time sample consists of the default years 2024–2025 (20,805 events). The out-of-time sample was not used for driver selection or pool design. After the pool design was fixed and tested, the LRA CCFs were calculated on the full RDS, because CRR Article 182(1)(a) requires the average of all observed defaults in the data sources. The development sample contains 12 years and the full RDS 14 years of default dates, which provides at least 6,305 events for the smallest pool and gives confidence in the accuracy and robustness of the estimates.

sections.heading: Methodological alternatives and selection
sections.text: Three approaches were assessed against the criteria of MRM-STD-020 §6.1 (regulatory compliance, data requirements, performance, stability, interpretability and implementation effort): (A) pooled LRA realised CCFs with a segmentation tree, (B) a fractional logit regression of the realised CCF on continuous drivers with pool assignment on the predicted CCF, and (C) retaining the v2.1 cohort approach with a conservative add-on. Approach C was rejected because it does not comply with CRR Article 182(1)(g). Approach B achieved a Somers' D of 0.262 on the out-of-time sample against 0.241 for approach A, but produced predicted CCFs outside [0,1] for 4.8% of facilities, required six drivers and was less stable across default years (Somers' D range 0.19–0.30 against 0.21–0.27). Approach A was selected because it is transparent, directly implements the default-weighted average of realised CCFs per pool required by CRR Article 182(1)(a), is stable and performs comparably; the performance difference to approach B is not material for the exposure value (EAD difference 0.6% at portfolio level).

Approach A was selected because it is transparent, directly implements the default-weighted average of realised CCFs per pool required by CRR Article 182(1)(a), is stable and performs comparably; the performance difference to approach B is not material for the exposure value (EAD difference 0.6% at portfolio level).

sections.heading: Realised CCF under the twelve-month fixed horizon
sections.text: Each default is linked to the obligor and facility characteristics at the reference date twelve months before the default date, and the realised CCF is calculated from the limit and drawn amount at that date and the EAD at the default date, as defined in RDS section 3.1. The realised CCFs of all observed defaults are used, including negative values and values far above 100%, which are neither floored nor capped at facility level; drawings after default are captured in the LGD model. Because the fixed horizon measures drawings over the full year before default, the estimates reflect additional drawings up to default, and customers' drawing behaviour in the months before default is visible in the RDS (median utilisation rises from 34% at the reference date to 88% at default for credit cards). The realised CCF depends on the Bank's account monitoring and payment processing: automatic limit reductions for high-risk card accounts (since 2019) and overdraft blocking at 60 days past due limit drawings short of default; realised CCFs of card defaults after 2019 are 3.4 percentage points lower than before, but because the policy is discretionary and could be relaxed, no reduction of the estimates for this effect is applied.

sections.heading: Candidate drivers and driver selection
sections.text: The long list of candidate drivers combined a literature review, the drivers of v2.1 and a workshop with Retail Collections and Retail Credit Risk Management on 9 July 2026: product, utilisation at reference date, delinquency status, limit size, account tenure, months since last limit increase, three-month balance trend, behavioural PD grade and number of cash withdrawals; the expected direction of each driver was recorded before estimation. Univariate analysis (Somers' D and monotonicity per driver) and a multivariate regression tree with minimum leaf size of 5,000 events were used; correlated drivers (utilisation and three-month balance trend, rank correlation 0.61) were treated by retaining the driver with higher stability over time. The final drivers are product (credit cards have higher realised CCFs than overdrafts at equal utilisation), utilisation at reference date (higher utilisation, higher CCF, consistent with the expected sign) and delinquency at reference date (1–89 dpd, higher CCF), which are all available at the point of use and stable over time. Limit size and behavioural PD grade were rejected because they added less than 0.005 to Somers' D and showed non-monotonic effects; account tenure was rejected in the proxy screening (RDS section 7.4) because of its association with age. The selected drivers reflect obligor characteristics (delinquency) and transaction characteristics (product and utilisation), and all relevant information available at the reference date was considered.

sections.heading: Pool definition
sections.text: Each facility with a committed limit is assigned monthly to one of ten pools: facilities with 1–89 days past due at the reference date are assigned to CC-5 (credit cards) or OD-5 (overdrafts); all other facilities are assigned by utilisation (drawn amount divided by limit) to band 1 (below 30%), band 2 (30% to below 70%), band 3 (70% to below 95%) or band 4 (95% and above), giving pools CC-1 to CC-4 and OD-1 to OD-4. The band boundaries of 30%, 70% and 95% were set by the developers by rounding the split points of the regression tree (28%, 66% and 94%), recorded as expert judgement EJ-CCF-01. The criteria use only system data and are applied identically to all facilities in all business lines and branches in scope, so similar facilities are assigned consistently to the same pool; the assignment is recalculated at every month-end and is therefore updated far more often than annually. Where the limit or the drawn amount is missing in production, the facility is assigned to the pool with the highest CCF for its product (CC-4 or OD-4), so that less information leads to a more conservative assignment. Pool sizes in the RDS range from 6,305 events (CC-4) to 38,410 events (OD-1), and in the application portfolio no pool holds more than 41% of the undrawn amount of its product.

sections.heading: Pool homogeneity and differentiation
sections.text: Differentiation between pools is tested with pairwise Welch t-tests of the mean realised CCF of adjacent pools on the development sample: all adjacent pools differ significantly at the 1% level, except CC-3 versus CC-5 (p = 0.03), which are kept separate because they differ in delinquency status and in their out-of-time CCF (79.9% against 85.6%). Homogeneity within pools is tested by splitting each pool by limit size, account tenure and default year: no subset of at least 1,000 events differs from the rest of its pool by more than 5 percentage points in mean realised CCF, except the 2013 default year in the overdraft pools, which is the downturn period treated in section 5.2. The Somers' D between the pool ranking and the realised CCF is 0.241 on the development sample, 0.238 out-of-sample and 0.228 out-of-time. The pooled approach thus provides a meaningful differentiation of risk and accurate and consistent estimates at pool level.

sections.heading: Long-run average CCF
sections.text: The LRA CCF of each pool is the default-weighted average of the realised CCFs of all default events in the pool over the full observation period 2012–2025, excluding only the 1,954 events with undefined CCF (DD-CCF-03). LRA CCFs are: CC-1 58.2%, CC-2 71.5%, CC-3 79.3%, CC-4 96.4%, CC-5 84.7%, OD-1 44.6%, OD-2 61.9%, OD-3 72.8%, OD-4 91.2% and OD-5 78.5%. The estimates are derived from historical experience and empirical evidence of all relevant data, with judgement limited to the choices recorded in the expert judgement log, and they are plausible and intuitive: CCFs rise with utilisation and delinquency, and credit card CCFs exceed overdraft CCFs because card limits are higher relative to income and are not blocked before 60 days past due. Changes in lending and account monitoring practice over the window (limit policy 2016, automatic limit reductions 2019, instant limit increases 2023) were analysed in section 4.2 and RDS section 5.1.2 and are reflected in the estimates or in MoC category B. No appropriate adjustment to the LRA was required; the bias from the approximated default flag (−0.3 percentage points) is not corrected because the corrected P3 benchmark is itself uncertain, and it is covered by MoC A-01.
