sections.heading: Downturn CCF
sections.text: The economic downturn for retail revolving exposures is identified in the downturn report EVD-03-DT (version 1.0, 27 November 2026) under Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/930, separately for this type of exposures: the relevant indicator set consists of Dutch real GDP, the unemployment rate, household debt, real disposable income and the BKR aggregate consumer credit default rate. Two downturn periods were identified: 2012Q2–2014Q1 (unemployment, BKR default rate, credit loss rate, household debt, disposable income and consumer confidence, merged into one period because these correlated indicators reached their most severe values within eight quarters) and 2019Q3–2020Q2 (GDP); the GDP contraction of 2008Q3–2009Q2 was assessed as a further candidate period. Because the effect on drawings appears with a lag, the downturn CCF is measured on defaults whose reference date falls within the downturn period, which shifts the observation window by about two quarters relative to the default dates; the period 2012Q2–2014Q1 shows the most elevated realised CCFs, while realised CCFs in 2020–2021 were lower than the LRA because of government support and lower spending. For the 2008–2009 period, which is not covered by the RDS, the impact was extrapolated with the unemployment sensitivity (+2.6 percentage points), which is lower than the observed impact of 2012–2014. The downturn add-on per pool is the difference between the default-weighted average realised CCF of the downturn period and the LRA, floored at zero: CC-1 +3.1, CC-2 +2.8, CC-3 +2.2, CC-4 +1.5, CC-5 +2.0, OD-1 +3.6, OD-2 +3.0, OD-3 +2.4, OD-4 +1.7 and OD-5 +2.1 percentage points; the downturn estimates are used because they are more conservative than the LRA in all pools. The positive correlation between default frequency and CCF magnitude is reflected by the downturn add-on, which is largest in the low-utilisation pools where drawings have most headroom, and by the MoC of section 6.

sections.heading: Final CCF, floors and exposure value
sections.text: The order of adjustments is: LRA CCF, plus downturn add-on, plus total MoC; the resulting pool CCF is floored at 0%; this order is applied identically in development and production. Final CCFs are: CC-1 63.3%, CC-2 76.5%, CC-3 83.9%, CC-4 101.3%, CC-5 89.3%, OD-1 50.4%, OD-2 67.3%, OD-3 77.8%, OD-4 96.4% and OD-5 83.4%. The exposure value of each facility is the drawn amount plus the final CCF times the undrawn amount, but not lower than the drawn amount plus 50% of the off-balance-sheet exposure value calculated with the Standardised Approach conversion factor of 10%, i.e. the drawn amount plus 5% of the undrawn amount, as required by CRR Article 166(8c). The floor is applied at facility level after MoC and downturn adjustment; at 31 December 2026 it is binding for 0.0% of facilities and EAD, because the lowest final CCF (50.4%) far exceeds 5%. For facilities with a drawn amount at or above the limit the undrawn amount is zero and the exposure value equals the drawn amount; the additional drawings of such facilities are covered by MoC A-03. The system calculating own funds requirements (RWA engine RiskCalc) applies the retail IRB risk weight formula for qualifying revolving retail exposures to the exposure value, and its implementation was tested as described in section 9.

sections.heading: MoC framework and identification of deficiencies
sections.text: The margin of conservatism follows CRM-STD-101 and EBA/GL/2017/16 section 4.4 as referred to by the ECB guide: the final estimate is the best estimate after appropriate adjustments plus a MoC that distinguishes category A (data and methodological deficiencies), category B (relevant changes) and category C (general estimation error). Deficiencies were identified systematically with the trigger list of CRM-STD-101 Annex 1 during development in August–September 2026; for each deficiency an appropriate adjustment was considered first, and the MoC is not used for deficiencies that can be corrected (the card snapshot gap DD-CCF-04 was corrected at source instead). Deficiencies considered and rejected are documented as well: the change of card processor in 2017 (no effect on limits and balances after the reload), the COVID-19 moratoria (payment holidays did not affect drawings) and the 2016 limit policy (lower limits make historical CCFs conservative). The two findings of the 2025 validation of v2.1 that relate to estimates (V25-03 on missing overdraft limit history and V25-05 on the treatment of over-limit accounts) were assessed and are included as A-02 and A-03. The ECB guide requirement that the MoC reflects estimation uncertainty at the level of the final pool estimates is met by quantifying every component per pool.

sections.heading: MoC category A
sections.text: A-01 (default flag approximation 2012–2015, DD-CCF-01): the parameter was re-estimated under three alternative treatments (excluding P1, shifting P1 default dates by the observed mean difference of 11 days, and applying the P3 relation between arrears and UTP); the adverse effect ranges from 0.1 to 0.4 percentage points and the MoC is set at 0.4 percentage points for all pools. A-02 (overdraft limit history, DD-CCF-02): the realised CCFs of the 2,904 affected events were recalculated with two alternative limit reconstructions (product maximum limit, and limit at migration without product default); the adverse effect on the LRA of the overdraft pools is at most 1.2 percentage points and the MoC is set at 1.2 percentage points for OD-1 to OD-5. A-01 is documented as permanent and reassessed annually; A-02 is permanent because the legacy data cannot be recovered; A-03 has a remediation plan to introduce an explicit treatment of over-limit facilities at the next recalibration (owner E. Smit, target date 31 December 2028).

sections.heading: MoC category B
sections.text: B-01 (instant limit increases via the mobile app since May 2023): customers can raise their card limit by up to EUR 1,500 without contact with the Bank, which increases available headroom but is only reflected in 2.5 years of default data. The MoC was quantified by comparing realised CCFs of card facilities that used the functionality within twelve months before default with those that did not (difference +2.8 percentage points on 1,640 events) and weighting it with the current share of card accounts using the function (31%), which gives 0.9 percentage points for CC-1 to CC-5. Because the quantification relies on a short period, the choice of weighting was recorded as expert judgement EJ-CCF-04 and approved under MRM-STD-023; statistical alternatives (bootstrapping the difference) gave 0.6–1.1 percentage points. No category B MoC is required for overdrafts: overdraft products, pricing and blocking rules have been unchanged since 2019, and no change in legal environment affecting drawings was identified.

sections.heading: MoC aggregation, register and effect
sections.text: The total MoC per pool is the simple sum of the category A, B and C components without diversification: CC-1 2.0, CC-2 2.2, CC-3 2.4, CC-4 3.4, CC-5 2.6, OD-1 2.2, OD-2 2.4, OD-3 2.6, OD-4 3.5 and OD-5 2.8 percentage points. Every component is non-negative, and no deficiency that lowers the estimate is used to offset another component. The MoC register MOC-REG-MDL03 records per deficiency the identifier, category, affected pools, quantification method, MoC value, link to the data deficiency log and remediation status. The total MoC is below 5 percentage points in all pools, so the redevelopment assessment of CRM-STD-101 §7.2 is not triggered. The MoC increases the RWEA of the rating system by EUR 14.6 million (category A 7.9, B 2.4, C 4.3), which is reported per category in the quarterly MoC report to the Model Risk Committee. The MoC is reviewed annually within the review of estimates (section 10.3); a component is reduced only after remediation is confirmed by Model Validation, and changes to the MoC are classified as model changes under MRM-STD-050.

sections.heading: Discriminatory power
sections.text: Discriminatory power is measured with Somers' D between the pool ranking (ordered by final CCF) and the realised CCF, which is the generalised AUC measure for CCF models of MV-HB-003 §5.5: 0.241 on the development sample, 0.238 out-of-sample and 0.228 out-of-time, a relative decrease of 5.4% (green, threshold 10%). Per product, Somers' D out-of-time is 0.236 for credit cards and 0.219 for overdrafts. The ranking of pools by mean realised CCF is identical in the development and out-of-time samples.

sections.heading: Calibration accuracy and back-testing
sections.text: Realised CCFs of the out-of-time sample are compared per pool with the LRA best estimate (before downturn and MoC) using a one-sided t-test against underestimation: no pool shows a significant underestimation at the 5% level; the lowest p-value is 0.08 for OD-4 (realised 92.9% against 91.2%). At portfolio level the realised CCF of the out-of-time sample is 68.9% for credit cards against an estimated 68.1% (relative underestimation 1.2%, green) and 56.4% for overdrafts against 57.2%. The EAD coverage ratio of the final estimates (estimated over realised EAD at default) is 1.07 for credit cards and 1.05 for overdrafts on the out-of-time sample. Back-testing uses the longest available history: an annual back-test of every default year 2012–2025 is included in Annex 7.2 and shows realised pool CCFs above the final CCF in 7 of 140 pool-years, all in 2013. All metrics are within their thresholds, so no entry in the limitations log was required under MRM-STD-020 §8.3.

sections.heading: Stability

Annual LRA CCFs per pool over 2012–2025 vary within ±4 percentage points of the LRA except in 2013; the pool ranking is stable in every year. Design stability was tested by re-estimating the regression tree on the first and second halves of the development period: the split points differ by at most 3 percentage points of utilisation from those of the full sample.

sections.heading: Sensitivity analysis
sections.text: Sensitivity analyses cover the key assumptions and choices: alternative utilisation boundaries (25/65/90 and 35/75/97: EAD change −0.4% and +0.3%), exclusion of the P1 default years (LRA −0.3 percentage points), alternative downturn period definitions (add-on 1.9 to 3.6 percentage points for CC-1), alternative treatment of reference dates for young accounts (EAD +0.2%), and the capping of realised CCFs at 100% for information (EAD −4.7%, not applied). The results are documented with their effect on the portfolio EAD and were used to support the MoC quantification in chapter 6. The sensitivity to the utilisation boundaries, which are an expert judgement, is below the medium materiality threshold of MRM-STD-023 §4.2.

sections.heading: Climate-related and environmental risks
sections.text: The materiality of climate-related and environmental risks for the conversion factors of unsecured retail revolving facilities was assessed qualitatively against the Bank's climate risk materiality assessment 2026: physical and transition risks affect drawings only indirectly through income and unemployment, which are captured by the downturn and stress-test approach, and no climate risk driver was included. A quantitative analysis linking realised CCFs to regional flood exposure was not performed because the postcode region is not a model driver.

sections.heading: Material assumptions
sections.text: The material assumptions are: (1) drawing behaviour in the year before default is stable enough over time for an LRA to be representative; (2) utilisation, product and delinquency at the reference date capture the main differences in drawing capacity; (3) the account monitoring practice will not become less restrictive than in the RDS period; (4) the downturn period 2012–2014 represents the most severe drawing behaviour; and (5) the reconstructed overdraft limits are unbiased on average. Assumptions 1 and 2 are supported by the stability tests of section 7.3, assumption 4 by the downturn report and assumption 5 by the sensitivity analysis of A-02. Assumption 3 is monitored through the annual review of estimates.

sections.heading: Circumstances in which the model does not work effectively
sections.text: The model is not suitable for facilities without a committed limit, for business overdrafts, for products with a contractual drawdown schedule or for portfolios whose limit management differs materially from the Bank's (for example acquired portfolios), and it may underestimate CCFs if automatic limit reductions or overdraft blocking were abandoned. Extending the model to such portfolios would be a change to the range of application requiring a representativeness assessment and classification under Delegated Regulation (EU) No 529/2014. A new product feature affecting drawing capacity, such as the 2023 instant limit increase, is assessed by the Model Owner for its effect on the estimates before launch through the new product approval process.

sections.heading: Production controls and parameter management
sections.text: The parameter table of final CCFs is version controlled in the RiskCalc parameter store with restricted access and is changed only through change management; model developers have no write access to the production environment. Every monthly production run logs the reference date, input data version, code version and parameter version and uses only the approved versions. Manual reruns and fallback procedures (use of the previous month's pool assignment if the card file is delayed) are documented in the RiskCalc operating manual and are authorised by the Head of Capital Reporting and logged.

sections.heading: Monitoring plan – KPIs and frequency
sections.text: The monitoring plan MP-CCF-REV-3.0, approved by the Model Owner and reviewed by Model Validation, defines the KPIs, their calculation, amber and red thresholds, frequency, data and reference periods, segments, responsible persons and escalation. KPIs are: PSI of the pool distribution and of utilisation and delinquency (semi-annual), Somers' D against development (annual), realised against estimated CCF per pool and for the portfolio (annual, fixed twelve-month horizon), EAD coverage ratio, production DQ of limit and balance fields, share of facilities assigned by the missing value rule (model coverage) and the overlay in place; overrides do not apply because pool assignment cannot be overridden. KPIs are calculated for the portfolio and for each pool, at least semi-annually as required for Tier 2 models, with calibration KPIs annually because of the twelve-month horizon. Results are reported within 60 calendar days after the reference period, with each KPI shown with value, threshold, traffic light and trend over the last four cycles, and monitoring code is version controlled in the tag mon-v3.0.0 so that results are reproducible. The monitoring plan is updated with every model change and reviewed annually.

sections.heading: Monitoring thresholds and escalation
sections.text: Thresholds follow MRM-STD-040: PSI green below 0.10, amber 0.10–0.25, red above 0.25; portfolio underestimation of the realised CCF above 5% relative amber and above 10% red; per pool, one-sided paired t-test p-value below 5% amber and below 1% red; relative decrease of Somers' D above 10% amber and above 20% red. Each amber result is analysed by the Model Owner and its cause documented; a red result or amber on the same KPI in two consecutive cycles is notified to MRM and Model Validation within ten business days, followed by a root cause analysis and action plan within 60 calendar days proposing no action with justification, an overlay, recalibration, redevelopment or restriction of use. A red outcome leads to a recalibration or redevelopment plan approved by the Model Risk Committee within three months, and monitoring results indicating non-compliance with the CRR are assessed for notification to the ECB and for an additional MoC. Monitoring results are provided to Credit Risk Management, which uses them in the retail credit risk reporting.

sections.heading: Annual review of estimates
sections.text: The estimates are reviewed at least annually and whenever new information comes to light, within the annual model review of the Model Owner: the review covers back-testing of realised against estimated CCFs per pool and for the portfolio over the longest available history, representativeness of the RDS for the current portfolio, the need for recalibration, the adequacy of the MoC, portfolio and environment changes, open findings and data deficiencies, the expert judgement log and overlays, and code-documentation consistency. The review concludes whether the model remains fit for purpose, is signed off by the Model Owner and submitted to MRM and Model Validation; the first review of v3.0 is planned for the reference date 31 December 2027. Internal standards for deviations: where realised CCFs exceed the estimates beyond the red threshold in a pool in two consecutive annual reviews, taking the position in the economic cycle into account, the estimates are revised upward at the next recalibration. The data window is extended annually with the latest default year; the MoC for the approximated default flag (A-01) is reassessed at each extension until a sufficiently long period under the current definition of default is available. Quantitative methods and data are kept consistent over time; any change in method, data source or period is documented in the annual review report.

sections.heading: Validation cycle
sections.text: As an IRB model the rating system is validated at least annually by Model Validation – Credit Risk, irrespective of its Tier 2 classification, with a full-scope validation at initial validation, after every material change and at least every three years. Model Validation is organisationally independent of Retail Credit Risk Modelling and of the business lines, reports to the CRO through the Head of Model Risk Management, and its staff did not contribute to the development of v3.0; the validation is based on its own analyses and data access. The rigorous statistical validation process for the model, including out-of-sample and out-of-time tests, is set out in this chapter and in chapter 7. The initial validation of v3.0 (G2) is planned for July–September 2027 and must precede the MRC approval and the application to the ECB.

sections.heading: Expert judgement log
sections.text: The expert judgement log EJ-LOG-MDL03 is stored with the model documentation in the repository and records every instance of expert judgement with type, life cycle stage, affected data, pool or parameter, rationale, evidence, alternatives considered, quantified impact, proposer, approver, approval date, review date and expiry conditions. The log contains five entries: EJ-CCF-01 utilisation boundaries (design; EAD impact 0.4%; low); EJ-CCF-02 combining all utilisation levels of delinquent facilities in one pool per product (design; 0.2%; low); EJ-CCF-03 two-quarter lag of the downturn window (calibration; EAD +0.9%; low); EJ-CCF-04 weighting of the B-01 MoC (MoC; EAD +0.5%; low); EJ-CCF-05 overdraft limit imputation rule (data treatment; see A-02; medium because its effect on the LRA of the overdraft pools is up to 1.2 percentage points). Each rationale refers to specific analyses (tree output, lag correlation, usage statistics) so that a third party can replicate its effect. All judgements are reviewed at each annual model review and when new data could replace them; no judgement has yet been withdrawn.

sections.heading: Overrides and overlays
sections.text: Pool assignment and CCFs cannot be overridden: the production process contains no override function, the closed list of override reasons for this rating system is empty, and the override rate is therefore monitored as zero. Human oversight of the model output is exercised through the monthly review of the EAD and RWEA movements by Capital Management and Retail Credit Risk Management, which checks for errors from model weaknesses using information not in the model, such as product changes. Since 1 January 2025 a post-model adjustment of +4.0 percentage points on the v2.1 CCFs addresses the non-compliance of v2.1 with the fixed-horizon requirement; it was quantified by comparing v2.1 CCFs with fixed-horizon realised CCFs on 2019–2023 defaults, approved by the Model Approval Panel on 12 December 2024 and is reported quarterly to the MRC. The need for the adjustment is reassessed semi-annually, and it will be removed when v3.0 goes live; because it will have been in place for more than 24 months by January 2027, the model change assessment of MRM-STD-023 §3.5 is fulfilled by the v3.0 change.

sections.heading: Regulatory status, remediation plan and next steps
sections.text: Because v2.1 does not comply with CRR Article 182(1)(g) since 1 January 2025, the Bank notified the ECB on 16 December 2024 and presented a plan to restore compliance with v3.0 by 31 March 2028, together with the interim post-model adjustment described in section 11.3; the plan is monitored quarterly by MRM and its execution is on schedule. The change from the cohort approach to the fixed-horizon approach is a change in the fundamental methodology for estimating conversion factors and is therefore classified as material (Class A) under Delegated Regulation (EU) No 529/2014; details are in the change memorandum EVD-03-CHG. After the initial validation, the model will be approved by the Model Risk Committee as a change requiring supervisory permission, with the material aspects approved by the Management Board on the MRC's recommendation, and v3.0 will be used for own funds requirements only after the ECB has granted permission. sections.heading: Purpose and intended use
sections.text: CCF-REV v3.0 estimates the conversion factors applied to the undrawn committed limits of retail credit cards and arranged current account overdrafts of natural persons, for the calculation of exposure values under the Advanced IRB approach (CRR Article 166(8a) to (8c) and Article 182). Version 3.0 replaces CCF-REV v2.1, which used a cohort approach with annual cohorts on 1 January; the cohort approach does not meet the twelve-month fixed-horizon requirement of CRR Article 182(1)(g), applicable since 1 January 2025 under Regulation (EU) 2024/1623, and the redevelopment implements that requirement. Secondary uses are the IFRS 9 lifetime EAD of the same portfolios (without MoC and downturn adjustment), the ICAAP economic capital model and the credit risk stress test. Users are Capital Management (own funds calculation), Retail Credit Risk Management (limit policy and risk appetite), Retail Pricing (risk-adjusted pricing of card products), Finance – Impairments and Enterprise Risk Management (ICAAP and stress testing). sections.heading: Range of application and exposure class
sections.text: The range of application comprises all credit card facilities (468,300 accounts, committed limits EUR 1,392 million, drawn EUR 341 million at 31 December 2026) and all current accounts with an arranged overdraft limit (1,104,900 accounts, limits EUR 1,268 million, drawn EUR 152 million) of natural persons booked by the Bank in the Netherlands. All facilities are revolving, unconditionally cancellable commitments that attract a 10% conversion factor under the Standardised Approach (CRR Article 111), so they are not subject to a 100% SA conversion factor and own estimates of conversion factors are permitted under CRR Article 166(8b). Exposures to institutions, financial sector entities and large corporates are outside the range of application, so the restriction of CRR Article 147a(1) on own CCF estimates for these exposures is respected by construction. The facilities are assigned to the retail exposure class by the exposure class assignment routine, which applies the CRR Article 147(5) and 154(4) criteria (natural persons, revolving, unsecured, total exposure to the obligor up to EUR 100,000, managed on a pooled basis) in a fixed sequence that has not changed since 2019. The IRB approach is applied to all retail exposures of the Bank; the credit card portfolio of the Belgian branch (3,100 accounts, EUR 11.8 million limits) is under permanent partial use of the Standardised Approach under CRR Article 150(1), approved by the ECB as immaterial in size and risk profile, and its share (0.4% of retail revolving limits) is monitored quarterly against the triggers of the roll-out plan (maximum 1% of the retail EAD). The roll-out plan agreed with the ECB has been completed for the retail exposure class, and no exposures are held back from the IRB approach to reduce own funds requirements.

sections.heading: Use of model outputs and internal parameters
sections.text: The CCF estimates play an essential role beyond own funds: the resulting EAD enters the internal capital allocation to the Retail Cards and Daily Banking business lines, the credit risk appetite metrics (expected loss and RWA density of retail unsecured lending), risk-adjusted pricing of card products, the calibration of limit policies (maximum initial limits and limit-increase rules) and the quarterly management reporting to the Retail Credit Committee. For IFRS 9 the Bank uses the same pools and realised CCFs but removes the MoC and the downturn add-on and applies a point-in-time adjustment; for pricing, the downturn add-on is also removed; these differences are documented and justified in the parameter mapping table PMT-CCF-2027 and the internal parameters are derived from the IRB parameters. The CCF is not used for decisions on individual customers: limit increase and approval decisions are based on the behavioural PD, policy rules and affordability, so the model does not produce automated individual decisions within the meaning of Article 22 GDPR. All risk parameters used for the risk appetite metrics of the retail unsecured portfolio are produced by models registered in the model inventory and approved under MRM-POL-001.

sections.heading: Model structure and components
sections.text: The rating system for conversion factors consists of four clearly separated components: (a) the assignment of each facility to one of ten CCF pools at the monthly reference date; (b) the long-run average (LRA) realised CCF per pool; (c) the downturn add-on per pool; and (d) the margin of conservatism per pool, followed by the application of the exposure value floor of CRR Article 166(8c) at facility level. The pools are defined by product (credit card, overdraft), utilisation band at the reference date and delinquency status at the reference date, as specified in section 4.4. The model is a statistical model developed in-house by Retail Credit Risk Modelling; no vendor model or proprietary third-party technology is used, and the external card processor provides data only. A third party can replicate the pool assignment from sections 4.4 and 5.3 and the implementation specification IS-CCF-REV-3.0 without further information.

sections.heading: Dependencies on other models
sections.text: The model depends on the retail behavioural PD model (MDL-02) only for the pool definition of delinquency status, which uses the dpd counter directly and not the PD, and on the default register for the default flag; it provides the EAD to the retail revolving LGD model (MDL-04), whose realised LGD includes drawings after default. Changes to the default definition therefore affect this model and are assessed as changes to all IRB rating systems under MRM-STD-050 and Delegated Regulation (EU) No 529/2014, as required by CR-STD-110 §10.3. The model complexity was assessed as Low in the ECB complexity assessment performed by MRM on 2 December 2025 (no machine learning, no dynamic recalibration). The model framework is governed by the Bank's written Model Risk Management Policy MRM-POL-001, which defines what constitutes a model and the components of the model risk framework.

sections.heading: Use in stress testing
sections.text: In the ICAAP and in the EBA and internal credit risk stress tests, the CCF per pool is stressed with the sensitivity of the quarterly average realised CCF to the unemployment rate estimated in the downturn report (EVD-03-DT, +0.9 percentage points per percentage point of unemployment), applied to the severe but plausible recession scenarios of the Bank's stress-testing framework. In the 2026 ICAAP adverse scenario (unemployment +3.8 percentage points) the stressed CCF increases the retail revolving EAD by 4.1% and the RWEA of the rating system by EUR 19 million; the result is part of the ICAAP report approved by the Management Board on 24 March 2027. The stress test covers the full range of application of the rating system.

sections.text: The model is developed on the frozen RDS RDS-CCF-REV-3.0 described in the approved RDS documentation EVD-03-RDS version 1.0 of 19 June 2026: 133,211 default events with default dates between January 2012 and December 2025, each linked to its reference date twelve months before default. The RDS stores for every defaulted facility the pool assignment data at the reference date, the realised CCF and the default date, and the production system stores the estimated CCF per pool and the pool of each facility in the twelve months before default, as required by CRR Article 176(4). Data deficiencies DD-CCF-01 to DD-CCF-03 of the RDS documentation are carried into the limitations log (L-01 to L-03) and the MoC register (A-01 to A-03). The same default definition is used for the CCF, PD and LGD models of the retail revolving rating system, so the RDS is consistent with the default events used in MDL-02 and MDL-04.

sections.heading: Development, out-of-sample and out-of-time samples
sections.text: Before any estimation, the samples were defined in the development plan: the development sample consists of the default years 2012–2023 (112,406 events), of which a random 30% hold-out stratified by product and default year is the out-of-sample (33,722 events), and the out-of-time sample consists of the default years 2024–2025 (20,805 events). The out-of-time sample was not used for driver selection or pool design. After the pool design was fixed and tested, the LRA CCFs were calculated on the full RDS, because CRR Article 182(1)(a) requires the average of all observed defaults in the data sources. The development sample contains 12 years and the full RDS 14 years of default dates, which provides at least 6,305 events for the smallest pool and gives confidence in the accuracy and robustness of the estimates.

sections.heading: Methodological alternatives and selection
sections.text: Three approaches were assessed against the criteria of MRM-STD-020 §6.1 (regulatory compliance, data requirements, performance, stability, interpretability and implementation effort): (A) pooled LRA realised CCFs with a segmentation tree, (B) a fractional logit regression of the realised CCF on continuous drivers with pool assignment on the predicted CCF, and (C) retaining the v2.1 cohort approach with a conservative add-on. Approach C was rejected because it does not comply with CRR Article 182(1)(g). Approach B achieved a Somers' D of 0.262 on the out-of-time sample against 0.241 for approach A, but produced predicted CCFs outside [0,1] for 4.8% of facilities, required six drivers and was less stable across default years (Somers' D range 0.19–0.30 against 0.21–0.27). Approach A was selected because it is transparent, directly implements the default-weighted average of realised CCFs per pool required by CRR Article 182(1)(a), is stable and performs comparably; the performance difference to approach B is not material for the exposure value (EAD difference 0.6% at portfolio level).

sections.heading: Realised CCF under the twelve-month fixed horizon
sections.text: Each default is linked to the obligor and facility characteristics at the reference date twelve months before the default date, and the realised CCF is calculated from the limit and drawn amount at that date and the EAD at the default date, as defined in RDS section 3.1. The realised CCFs of all observed defaults are used, including negative values and values far above 100%, which are neither floored nor capped at facility level; drawings after default are captured in the LGD model. Because the fixed horizon measures drawings over the full year before default, the estimates reflect additional drawings up to default, and customers' drawing behaviour in the months before default is visible in the RDS (median utilisation rises from 34% at the reference date to 88% at default for credit cards). The realised CCF depends on the Bank's account monitoring and payment processing: automatic limit reductions for high-risk card accounts (since 2019) and overdraft blocking at 60 days past due limit drawings short of default; realised CCFs of card defaults after 2019 are 3.4 percentage points lower than before, but because the policy is discretionary and could be relaxed, no reduction of the estimates for this effect is applied.

sections.heading: Candidate drivers and driver selection
sections.text: The long list of candidate drivers combined a literature review, the drivers of v2.1 and a workshop with Retail Collections and Retail Credit Risk Management on 9 July 2026: product, utilisation at reference date, delinquency status, limit size, account tenure, months since last limit increase, three-month balance trend, behavioural PD grade and number of cash withdrawals; the expected direction of each driver was recorded before estimation. Univariate analysis (Somers' D and monotonicity per driver) and a multivariate regression tree with minimum leaf size of 5,000 events were used; correlated drivers (utilisation and three-month balance trend, rank correlation 0.61) were treated by retaining the driver with higher stability over time. The final drivers are product (credit cards have higher realised CCFs than overdrafts at equal utilisation), utilisation at reference date (higher utilisation, higher CCF, consistent with the expected sign) and delinquency at reference date (1–89 dpd, higher CCF), which are all available at the point of use and stable over time. Limit size and behavioural PD grade were rejected because they added less than 0.005 to Somers' D and showed non-monotonic effects; account tenure was rejected in the proxy screening (RDS section 7.4) because of its association with age. The selected drivers reflect obligor characteristics (delinquency) and transaction characteristics (product and utilisation), and all relevant information available at the reference date was considered.

sections.heading: Pool definition
sections.text: Each facility with a committed limit is assigned monthly to one of ten pools: facilities with 1–89 days past due at the reference date are assigned to CC-5 (credit cards) or OD-5 (overdrafts); all other facilities are assigned by utilisation (drawn amount divided by limit) to band 1 (below 30%), band 2 (30% to below 70%), band 3 (70% to below 95%) or band 4 (95% and above), giving pools CC-1 to CC-4 and OD-1 to OD-4. The band boundaries of 30%, 70% and 95% were set by the developers by rounding the split points of the regression tree (28%, 66% and 94%), recorded as expert judgement EJ-CCF-01. The criteria use only system data and are applied identically to all facilities in all business lines and branches in scope, so similar facilities are assigned consistently to the same pool; the assignment is recalculated at every month-end and is therefore updated far more often than annually. Where the limit or the drawn amount is missing in production, the facility is assigned to the pool with the highest CCF for its product (CC-4 or OD-4), so that less information leads to a more conservative assignment. Pool sizes in the RDS range from 6,305 events (CC-4) to 38,410 events (OD-1), and in the application portfolio no pool holds more than 41% of the undrawn amount of its product.

sections.heading: Pool homogeneity and differentiation
sections.text: Differentiation between pools is tested with pairwise Welch t-tests of the mean realised CCF of adjacent pools on the development sample: all adjacent pools differ significantly at the 1% level, except CC-3 versus CC-5 (p = 0.03), which are kept separate because they differ in delinquency status and in their out-of-time CCF (79.9% against 85.6%). Homogeneity within pools is tested by splitting each pool by limit size, account tenure and default year: no subset of at least 1,000 events differs from the rest of its pool by more than 5 percentage points in mean realised CCF, except the 2013 default year in the overdraft pools, which is the downturn period treated in section 5.2. The Somers' D between the pool ranking and the realised CCF is 0.241 on the development sample, 0.238 out-of-sample and 0.228 out-of-time. The pooled approach thus provides a meaningful differentiation of risk and accurate and consistent estimates at pool level.

sections.heading: Long-run average CCF
sections.text: The LRA CCF of each pool is the default-weighted average of the realised CCFs of all default events in the pool over the full observation period 2012–2025, excluding only the 1,954 events with undefined CCF (DD-CCF-03). LRA CCFs are: CC-1 58.2%, CC-2 71.5%, CC-3 79.3%, CC-4 96.4%, CC-5 84.7%, OD-1 44.6%, OD-2 61.9%, OD-3 72.8%, OD-4 91.2% and OD-5 78.5%. The estimates are derived from historical experience and empirical evidence of all relevant data, with judgement limited to the choices recorded in the expert judgement log, and they are plausible and intuitive: CCFs rise with utilisation and delinquency, and credit card CCFs exceed overdraft CCFs because card limits are higher relative to income and are not blocked before 60 days past due. Changes in lending and account monitoring practice over the window (limit policy 2016, automatic limit reductions 2019, instant limit increases 2023) were analysed in section 4.2 and RDS section 5.1.2 and are reflected in the estimates or in MoC category B. No appropriate adjustment to the LRA was required; the bias from the approximated default flag (−0.3 percentage points) is not corrected because the corrected P3 benchmark is itself uncertain, and it is covered by MoC A-01.

sections.heading: Downturn CCF
sections.text: The economic downturn for retail revolving exposures is identified in the downturn report EVD-03-DT (version 1.0, 27 November 2026) under Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/930, separately for this type of exposures: the relevant indicator set consists of Dutch real GDP, the unemployment rate, household debt, real disposable income and the BKR aggregate consumer credit default rate. Two downturn periods were identified: 2012Q2–2014Q1 (unemployment, BKR default rate, credit loss rate, household debt, disposable income and consumer confidence, merged into one period because these correlated indicators reached their most severe values within eight quarters) and 2019Q3–2020Q2 (GDP); the GDP contraction of 2008Q3–2009Q2 was assessed as a further candidate period. Because the effect on drawings appears with a lag, the downturn CCF is measured on defaults whose reference date falls within the downturn period, which shifts the observation window by about two quarters relative to the default dates; the period 2012Q2–2014Q1 shows the most elevated realised CCFs, while realised CCFs in 2020–2021 were lower than the LRA because of government support and lower spending. For the 2008–2009 period, which is not covered by the RDS, the impact was extrapolated with the unemployment sensitivity (+2.6 percentage points), which is lower than the observed impact of 2012–2014. The downturn add-on per pool is the difference between the default-weighted average realised CCF of the downturn period and the LRA, floored at zero: CC-1 +3.1, CC-2 +2.8, CC-3 +2.2, CC-4 +1.5, CC-5 +2.0, OD-1 +3.6, OD-2 +3.0, OD-3 +2.4, OD-4 +1.7 and OD-5 +2.1 percentage points; the downturn estimates are used because they are more conservative than the LRA in all pools. The positive correlation between default frequency and CCF magnitude is reflected by the downturn add-on, which is largest in the low-utilisation pools where drawings have most headroom, and by the MoC of section 6.

sections.heading: Final CCF, floors and exposure value
sections.text: The order of adjustments is: LRA CCF, plus downturn add-on, plus total MoC; the resulting pool CCF is floored at 0%; this order is applied identically in development and production. Final CCFs are: CC-1 63.3%, CC-2 76.5%, CC-3 83.9%, CC-4 101.3%, CC-5 89.3%, OD-1 50.4%, OD-2 67.3%, OD-3 77.8%, OD-4 96.4% and OD-5 83.4%. The exposure value of each facility is the drawn amount plus the final CCF times the undrawn amount, but not lower than the drawn amount plus 50% of the off-balance-sheet exposure value calculated with the Standardised Approach conversion factor of 10%, i.e. the drawn amount plus 5% of the undrawn amount, as required by CRR Article 166(8c). The floor is applied at facility level after MoC and downturn adjustment; at 31 December 2026 it is binding for 0.0% of facilities and EAD, because the lowest final CCF (50.4%) far exceeds 5%. For facilities with a drawn amount at or above the limit the undrawn amount is zero and the exposure value equals the drawn amount; the additional drawings of such facilities are covered by MoC A-03. The system calculating own funds requirements (RWA engine RiskCalc) applies the retail IRB risk weight formula for qualifying revolving retail exposures to the exposure value, and its implementation was tested as described in section 9.

The system calculating own funds requirements (RWA engine RiskCalc) applies the retail IRB risk weight formula for qualifying revolving retail exposures to the exposure value, and its implementation was tested as described in section 9.

sections.heading: MoC framework and identification of deficiencies
sections.text: The margin of conservatism follows CRM-STD-101 and EBA/GL/2017/16 section 4.4 as referred to by the ECB guide: the final estimate is the best estimate after appropriate adjustments plus a MoC that distinguishes category A (data and methodological deficiencies), category B (relevant changes) and category C (general estimation error). Deficiencies were identified systematically with the trigger list of CRM-STD-101 Annex 1 during development in August–September 2026; for each deficiency an appropriate adjustment was considered first, and the MoC is not used for deficiencies that can be corrected (the card snapshot gap DD-CCF-04 was corrected at source instead). Deficiencies considered and rejected are documented as well: the change of card processor in 2017 (no effect on limits and balances after the reload), the COVID-19 moratoria (payment holidays did not affect drawings) and the 2016 limit policy (lower limits make historical CCFs conservative). The two findings of the 2025 validation of v2.1 that relate to estimates (V25-03 on missing overdraft limit history and V25-05 on the treatment of over-limit accounts) were assessed and are included as A-02 and A-03. The ECB guide requirement that the MoC reflects estimation uncertainty at the level of the final pool estimates is met by quantifying every component per pool.

sections.heading: MoC category A
sections.text: A-01 (default flag approximation 2012–2015, DD-CCF-01): the parameter was re-estimated under three alternative treatments (excluding P1, shifting P1 default dates by the observed mean difference of 11 days, and applying the P3 relation between arrears and UTP); the adverse effect ranges from 0.1 to 0.4 percentage points and the MoC is set at 0.4 percentage points for all pools. A-02 (overdraft limit history, DD-CCF-02): the realised CCFs of the 2,904 affected events were recalculated with two alternative limit reconstructions (product maximum limit, and limit at migration without product default); the adverse effect on the LRA of the overdraft pools is at most 1.2 percentage points and the MoC is set at 1.2 percentage points for OD-1 to OD-5. A-03 (over-limit facilities with undefined CCF, DD-CCF-03): the average additional drawing of these facilities of 3.1% of the limit, expressed relative to the undrawn amounts of pools CC-4 and OD-4, corresponds to 0.5 percentage points, which is the MoC for these two pools. In each case the MoC is not lower than the adverse effect indicated by the sensitivity analysis. A-01 is documented as permanent and reassessed annually; A-02 is permanent because the legacy data cannot be recovered; A-03 has a remediation plan to introduce an explicit treatment of over-limit facilities at the next recalibration (owner E. Smit, target date 31 December 2028). Because more than 17% of the RDS relies on approximated or reconstructed data, the MoC for A-01 and A-02 was set at the upper end of the sensitivity range, reflecting that the less satisfactory the data, the larger the margin.

sections.heading: MoC category B
sections.text: B-01 (instant limit increases via the mobile app since May 2023): customers can raise their card limit by up to EUR 1,500 without contact with the Bank, which increases available headroom but is only reflected in 2.5 years of default data. The MoC was quantified by comparing realised CCFs of card facilities that used the functionality within twelve months before default with those that did not (difference +2.8 percentage points on 1,640 events) and weighting it with the current share of card accounts using the function (31%), which gives 0.9 percentage points for CC-1 to CC-5. Because the quantification relies on a short period, the choice of weighting was recorded as expert judgement EJ-CCF-04 and approved under MRM-STD-023; statistical alternatives (bootstrapping the difference) gave 0.6–1.1 percentage points. No category B MoC is required for overdrafts: overdraft products, pricing and blocking rules have been unchanged since 2019, and no change in legal environment affecting drawings was identified.

sections.heading: MoC aggregation, register and effect
sections.text: The total MoC per pool is the simple sum of the category A, B and C components without diversification: CC-1 2.0, CC-2 2.2, CC-3 2.4, CC-4 3.4, CC-5 2.6, OD-1 2.2, OD-2 2.4, OD-3 2.6, OD-4 3.5 and OD-5 2.8 percentage points. Every component is non-negative, and no deficiency that lowers the estimate is used to offset another component. The MoC register MOC-REG-MDL03 records per deficiency the identifier, category, affected pools, quantification method, MoC value, link to the data deficiency log and remediation status. The total MoC is below 5 percentage points in all pools, so the redevelopment assessment of CRM-STD-101 §7.2 is not triggered. The MoC increases the RWEA of the rating system by EUR 14.6 million (category A 7.9, B 2.4, C 4.3), which is reported per category in the quarterly MoC report to the Model Risk Committee. The MoC is reviewed annually within the review of estimates (section 10.3); a component is reduced only after remediation is confirmed by Model Validation, and changes to the MoC are classified as model changes under MRM-STD-050.

sections.heading: Discriminatory power
sections.text: Discriminatory power is measured with Somers' D between the pool ranking (ordered by final CCF) and the realised CCF, which is the generalised AUC measure for CCF models of MV-HB-003 §5.5: 0.241 on the development sample, 0.238 out-of-sample and 0.228 out-of-time, a relative decrease of 5.4% (green, threshold 10%). Per product, Somers' D out-of-time is 0.236 for credit cards and 0.219 for overdrafts. The ranking of pools by mean realised CCF is identical in the development and out-of-time samples.

sections.heading: Calibration accuracy and back-testing
sections.text: Realised CCFs of the out-of-time sample are compared per pool with the LRA best estimate (before downturn and MoC) using a one-sided t-test against underestimation: no pool shows a significant underestimation at the 5% level; the lowest p-value is 0.08 for OD-4 (realised 92.9% against 91.2%). At portfolio level the realised CCF of the out-of-time sample is 68.9% for credit cards against an estimated 68.1% (relative underestimation 1.2%, green) and 56.4% for overdrafts against 57.2%. The EAD coverage ratio of the final estimates (estimated over realised EAD at default) is 1.07 for credit cards and 1.05 for overdrafts on the out-of-time sample. Back-testing uses the longest available history: an annual back-test of every default year 2012–2025 is included in Annex 7.2 and shows realised pool CCFs above the final CCF in 7 of 140 pool-years, all in 2013. All metrics are within their thresholds, so no entry in the limitations log was required under MRM-STD-020 §8.3.

sections.heading: Benchmarking
sections.text: As a Tier 2 model, CCF-REV v3.0 is compared with its predecessor v2.1 and with the fractional logit challenger of section 4.1. Against v2.1, the new model increases the portfolio EAD by 3.9% and the RWEA by 6.8%, mainly because the fixed horizon captures drawings of accounts that were opened or increased less than twelve months before 1 January cohorts, and because v2.1 had no explicit downturn add-on; the credit card pools show the larger increase (+8.9% RWEA). The challenger outperforms the model on Somers' D by 0.021; the model was nevertheless selected for the reasons in section 4.1, and the EAD difference between model and challenger is 0.6%. An external comparison with the CCF estimates published in the Pillar 3 reports of four Dutch and Belgian IRB banks (range 45–78% for qualifying revolving retail) places the portfolio-average final CCF of 63.8% within the range. The comparison with the Pillar 3 figures is indicative only, because definitions of the reported CCF differ.

sections.heading: Sensitivity analysis
sections.text: Sensitivity analyses cover the key assumptions and choices: alternative utilisation boundaries (25/65/90 and 35/75/97: EAD change −0.4% and +0.3%), exclusion of the P1 default years (LRA −0.3 percentage points), alternative downturn period definitions (add-on 1.9 to 3.6 percentage points for CC-1), alternative treatment of reference dates for young accounts (EAD +0.2%), and the capping of realised CCFs at 100% for information (EAD −4.7%, not applied). The results are documented with their effect on the portfolio EAD and were used to support the MoC quantification in chapter 6. The sensitivity to the utilisation boundaries, which are an expert judgement, is below the medium materiality threshold of MRM-STD-023 §4.2.

sections.heading: Climate-related and environmental risks
sections.text: The materiality of climate-related and environmental risks for the conversion factors of unsecured retail revolving facilities was assessed qualitatively against the Bank's climate risk materiality assessment 2026: physical and transition risks affect drawings only indirectly through income and unemployment, which are captured by the downturn and stress-test approach, and no climate risk driver was included. A quantitative analysis linking realised CCFs to regional flood exposure was not performed because the postcode region is not a model driver.

sections.heading: Material assumptions
sections.text: The material assumptions are: (1) drawing behaviour in the year before default is stable enough over time for an LRA to be representative; (2) utilisation, product and delinquency at the reference date capture the main differences in drawing capacity; (3) the account monitoring practice will not become less restrictive than in the RDS period; (4) the downturn period 2012–2014 represents the most severe drawing behaviour; and (5) the reconstructed overdraft limits are unbiased on average. Assumptions 1 and 2 are supported by the stability tests of section 7.3, assumption 4 by the downturn report and assumption 5 by the sensitivity analysis of A-02. Assumption 3 is monitored through the annual review of estimates.

sections.heading: Circumstances in which the model does not work effectively
sections.text: The model is not suitable for facilities without a committed limit, for business overdrafts, for products with a contractual drawdown schedule or for portfolios whose limit management differs materially from the Bank's (for example acquired portfolios), and it may underestimate CCFs if automatic limit reductions or overdraft blocking were abandoned. Extending the model to such portfolios would be a change to the range of application requiring a representativeness assessment and classification under Delegated Regulation (EU) No 529/2014. A new product feature affecting drawing capacity, such as the 2023 instant limit increase, is assessed by the Model Owner for its effect on the estimates before launch through the new product approval process.

sections.heading: Implementation specification and handover
sections.text: The implementation specification IS-CCF-REV-3.0 (approved by the Model Owner on 18 December 2026) defines the production source field of every input, the pool assignment rules, the missing value rule, the parameter table of final CCFs, the floor and the rounding conventions (CCF to four decimals), consistent with this MDD. The handover package contained the specification, the parameter table, 1,200 test cases with expected outputs generated with the development code (covering every pool, the band boundaries, missing and invalid inputs) and reference outputs for the full RDS. Implementation testing, the reconciliation of production and development outputs and the parallel run are documented in the implementation and testing report EVD-03-IMPL. The production code, the implementation specification and this MDD were confirmed consistent by the Model Owner on 30 April 2027.

sections.heading: Production controls and parameter management
sections.text: The parameter table of final CCFs is version controlled in the RiskCalc parameter store with restricted access and is changed only through change management; model developers have no write access to the production environment. Every monthly production run logs the reference date, input data version, code version and parameter version and uses only the approved versions. Manual reruns and fallback procedures (use of the previous month's pool assignment if the card file is delayed) are documented in the RiskCalc operating manual and are authorised by the Head of Capital Reporting and logged.

sections.heading: Monitoring plan – KPIs and frequency
sections.text: The monitoring plan MP-CCF-REV-3.0, approved by the Model Owner and reviewed by Model Validation, defines the KPIs, their calculation, amber and red thresholds, frequency, data and reference periods, segments, responsible persons and escalation. KPIs are: PSI of the pool distribution and of utilisation and delinquency (semi-annual), Somers' D against development (annual), realised against estimated CCF per pool and for the portfolio (annual, fixed twelve-month horizon), EAD coverage ratio, production DQ of limit and balance fields, share of facilities assigned by the missing value rule (model coverage) and the overlay in place; overrides do not apply because pool assignment cannot be overridden. KPIs are calculated for the portfolio and for each pool, at least semi-annually as required for Tier 2 models, with calibration KPIs annually because of the twelve-month horizon. Results are reported within 60 calendar days after the reference period, with each KPI shown with value, threshold, traffic light and trend over the last four cycles, and monitoring code is version controlled in the tag mon-v3.0.0 so that results are reproducible. The monitoring plan is updated with every model change and reviewed annually.

sections.heading: Monitoring thresholds and escalation
sections.text: Thresholds follow MRM-STD-040: PSI green below 0.10, amber 0.10–0.25, red above 0.25; portfolio underestimation of the realised CCF above 5% relative amber and above 10% red; per pool, one-sided paired t-test p-value below 5% amber and below 1% red; relative decrease of Somers' D above 10% amber and above 20% red. Each amber result is analysed by the Model Owner and its cause documented; a red result or amber on the same KPI in two consecutive cycles is notified to MRM and Model Validation within ten business days, followed by a root cause analysis and action plan within 60 calendar days proposing no action with justification, an overlay, recalibration, redevelopment or restriction of use. A red outcome leads to a recalibration or redevelopment plan approved by the Model Risk Committee within three months, and monitoring results indicating non-compliance with the CRR are assessed for notification to the ECB and for an additional MoC. Monitoring results are provided to Credit Risk Management, which uses them in the retail credit risk reporting.

sections.heading: Annual review of estimates
sections.text: The estimates are reviewed at least annually and whenever new information comes to light, within the annual model review of the Model Owner: the review covers back-testing of realised against estimated CCFs per pool and for the portfolio over the longest available history, representativeness of the RDS for the current portfolio, the need for recalibration, the adequacy of the MoC, portfolio and environment changes, open findings and data deficiencies, the expert judgement log and overlays, and code-documentation consistency. The review concludes whether the model remains fit for purpose, is signed off by the Model Owner and submitted to MRM and Model Validation; the first review of v3.0 is planned for the reference date 31 December 2027. Internal standards for deviations: where realised CCFs exceed the estimates beyond the red threshold in a pool in two consecutive annual reviews, taking the position in the economic cycle into account, the estimates are revised upward at the next recalibration. The data window is extended annually with the latest default year; the MoC for the approximated default flag (A-01) is reassessed at each extension until a sufficiently long period under the current definition of default is available. Quantitative methods and data are kept consistent over time; any change in method, data source or period is documented in the annual review report.

sections.heading: Validation cycle
sections.text: As an IRB model the rating system is validated at least annually by Model Validation – Credit Risk, irrespective of its Tier 2 classification, with a full-scope validation at initial validation, after every material change and at least every three years. Model Validation is organisationally independent of Retail Credit Risk Modelling and of the business lines, reports to the CRO through the Head of Model Risk Management, and its staff did not contribute to the development of v3.0; the validation is based on its own analyses and data access. The rigorous statistical validation process for the model, including out-of-sample and out-of-time tests, is set out in this chapter and in chapter 7. The initial validation of v3.0 (G2) is planned for July–September 2027 and must precede the MRC approval and the application to the ECB.

sections.heading: Expert judgement log
sections.text: The expert judgement log EJ-LOG-MDL03 is stored with the model documentation in the repository and records every instance of expert judgement with type, life cycle stage, affected data, pool or parameter, rationale, evidence, alternatives considered, quantified impact, proposer, approver, approval date, review date and expiry conditions. The log contains five entries: EJ-CCF-01 utilisation boundaries (design; EAD impact 0.4%; low); EJ-CCF-02 combining all utilisation levels of delinquent facilities in one pool per product (design; 0.2%; low); EJ-CCF-03 two-quarter lag of the downturn window (calibration; EAD +0.9%; low); EJ-CCF-04 weighting of the B-01 MoC (MoC; EAD +0.5%; low); EJ-CCF-05 overdraft limit imputation rule (data treatment; see A-02; medium because its effect on the LRA of the overdraft pools is up to 1.2 percentage points). Each rationale refers to specific analyses (tree output, lag correlation, usage statistics) so that a third party can replicate its effect. All judgements are reviewed at each annual model review and when new data could replace them; no judgement has yet been withdrawn.

sections.text: Low materiality judgements were approved by the Model Owner, and EJ-CCF-05 (medium) by the Model Owner and the Head of Retail Credit Risk Modelling on 24 September 2026, after documented challenge by R. Jansen, who was independent of the proposer; in no case was the proposer the sole approver. No expert panel was used. Human judgement in the model is limited to these design and calibration choices and is justified and documented, and its impact is quantified by sensitivity analysis.

sections.heading: Overrides and overlays
sections.text: Pool assignment and CCFs cannot be overridden: the production process contains no override function, the closed list of override reasons for this rating system is empty, and the override rate is therefore monitored as zero. Human oversight of the model output is exercised through the monthly review of the EAD and RWEA movements by Capital Management and Retail Credit Risk Management, which checks for errors from model weaknesses using information not in the model, such as product changes. Since 1 January 2025 a post-model adjustment of +4.0 percentage points on the v2.1 CCFs addresses the non-compliance of v2.1 with the fixed-horizon requirement; it was quantified by comparing v2.1 CCFs with fixed-horizon realised CCFs on 2019–2023 defaults, approved by the Model Approval Panel on 12 December 2024 and is reported quarterly to the MRC. The need for the adjustment is reassessed semi-annually, and it will be removed when v3.0 goes live; because it will have been in place for more than 24 months by January 2027, the model change assessment of MRM-STD-023 §3.5 is fulfilled by the v3.0 change.

sections.heading: Approvals and sign-offs

sections.heading: Regulatory status, remediation plan and next steps
sections.text: Because v2.1 does not comply with CRR Article 182(1)(g) since 1 January 2025, the Bank notified the ECB on 16 December 2024 and presented a plan to restore compliance with v3.0 by 31 March 2028, together with the interim post-model adjustment described in section 11.3; the plan is monitored quarterly by MRM and its execution is on schedule. The change from the cohort approach to the fixed-horizon approach is a change in the fundamental methodology for estimating conversion factors and is therefore classified as material (Class A) under Delegated Regulation (EU) No 529/2014; details are in the change memorandum EVD-03-CHG. After the initial validation, the model will be approved by the Model Risk Committee as a change requiring supervisory permission, with the material aspects approved by the Management Board on the MRC's recommendation, and v3.0 will be used for own funds requirements only after the ECB has granted permission. Condition C-2025-044 of the 2025 validation of v2.1 (implement the fixed-horizon approach) is recorded in the MRC conditions register with owner M. de Vries and deadline 31 March 2028, and the remediation plans for the medium findings V25-03 and V25-05 were submitted within 20 business days of the validation report.

sections.heading: Scope and approach
sections.text: This report documents the data quality assessment of the RDS RDS-CCF-REV-3.0 for the conversion factor model CCF-REV v3.0 (MDL-03), performed between 4 May and 12 June 2026 by Retail Credit Risk Modelling with support of the Retail Data Quality team, before the RDS was frozen and before estimation started. The assessment applies the Data Quality Standard for Models MRM-STD-022 v2.2, which implements the Bank's data quality management framework for all data used in IRB processes, including internal data from third-party processors. The framework is part of the Bank's data governance under DATA-POL-001, which applies chapter 3.2 of the ECB Guide on effective risk data aggregation and risk reporting to all model input data, and is approved by the Management Board as part of the Group data strategy. Dimensions assessed are completeness, accuracy, consistency, timeliness, validity, uniqueness and appropriateness for the range of application.

sections.heading: Critical data elements and DQ rules
sections.text: Eleven critical data elements (CDEs) were defined: limit and drawn balance at reference date, balance at default, default flag, default date, dpd counter, product type, account open date, obligor key, limit change history and write-off amount; for each CDE at least one DQ rule is defined per applicable mandatory dimension, and where a dimension does not apply the reason is recorded (for example timeliness is not applicable to the static product type). The 58 DQ rules are listed in Annex 1 of this report and in RDS Annex A; the 41 recurring rules are implemented in the Group DQ monitoring tool DQ Monitor for the monthly production data. DQ checks operate from data entry to reporting: input validations in Core24 and in the processor interface, reconciliations within RDW between staging and core layers, and reconciliations between risk data and the finance ledger. Controls over these risk data follow the same four-eyes and reconciliation standards as accounting data, and manual workarounds are limited to the two version-controlled input files described in RDS section 4.1.2.

sections.heading: Thresholds
sections.text: Each DQ rule has an amber and a red threshold equal to or stricter than the defaults of MRM-STD-022 §4.3: completeness amber below 98% and red below 95% non-missing, accuracy amber above 0.5% and red above 1% difference in amount, consistency amber below 99% and red below 98% of records passing. For the constituents of the target variable (balance at default, default flag, default date, limit and drawn amount at reference date) stricter thresholds apply: completeness amber below 99.5% and red below 99%, accuracy of amounts amber above 0.25% and red above 0.5%. No threshold less strict than the default is used, so no deviation needed approval.

sections.heading: Completeness
sections.text: Record-level completeness was verified by comparing the facilities in the RDS panel with the in-scope population of the source systems per month-end, and the default events with the default register: all 146,382 facility default events in scope with default dates 2012–2025 are present before exclusions, and no month-end snapshot is missing after the reload of the two 2017 card snapshots. Attribute-level completeness is above 99.8% for all CDEs except the overdraft limit at reference date for 2012–2014 (97.9%, amber) and the limit change history (97.1%, structural gaps for young accounts). The completeness gap of the overdraft limit is explained by the CBS-L migration and its impact on the reliability of the realised CCF is assessed in RDS section 6.2 (DD-CCF-02).

sections.heading: Accuracy and reconciliation
sections.text: Accuracy was measured by reconciliation of drawn balances and limits per year-end snapshot to the finance ledger and to the processor settlement totals (maximum difference 0.08% of amount), by comparison of default events with the default register maintained under CR-STD-110 (100% match after exclusion of technical past due events), and by sample checks. Although sample-based verification is mandatory only for Tier 1 models, 200 randomly drawn default events were verified against account statements and collection files; 198 agreed in full and two showed a default date difference of one day caused by weekend processing. The critical data elements are reconciled against source systems and the ledger at least annually as part of the annual model review, and unexplained differences are recorded as data quality issues. The RDS is therefore reconcilable with the accounting data and with the data used in the COREP credit risk reports of 31 December 2025.

sections.heading: Consistency
sections.text: Consistency was assessed between related fields (drawn balance not above limit plus authorised over-limit margin for 99.4% of records; default date not before account open date for 100%), over the observation period (distributions per year and per dod_regime, including the change in default definition in December 2020), and between the RDS and the production input data of the current model for the months January–December 2025 (99.97% agreement of limit and balance). The 0.6% of records with a balance above the limit plus margin are genuine over-limit positions confirmed by the processor and are retained. Obligors holding both a credit card and an overdraft are identified through the common Group customer key, so each obligor-level default is recorded once per facility and not duplicated across source systems.

sections.heading: Timeliness, validity and uniqueness
sections.text: Timeliness: month-end snapshots are available in RDW on the fifth business day after the reference date; the processor file for credit cards arrives by the third business day; the default register is updated daily; all are within the timeliness thresholds. Validity: all product codes, currency codes and dpd values are within their permitted domains after the mapping of the 43 legacy CBS-L product codes. Uniqueness: 1,033 duplicate facility records caused by the Core24 migration were identified and removed (exclusion E3); no other duplicates exist on the key facility–month. Appropriateness: the RDS covers all facilities of the range of application and is representative of the application portfolio as shown in RDS chapter 5. The data architecture of RDW supports the aggregation of these data fully and with the same timeliness in stress situations, as tested in the Bank's BCBS 239 annual self-assessment 2025.

sections.heading: Deficiencies, issues and escalation
sections.text: Four data quality incidents were recorded in the data issue register with an appointed owner and a priority-based action plan: DIR-2026-0412 (default flag approximation, accepted, mitigated by MoC), DIR-2026-0413 (overdraft limit history, not remediable at source, mitigated by imputation and MoC), DIR-2026-0414 (undefined CCF for over-limit accounts, methodological) and DIR-2026-0415 (missing 2017 card snapshots, resolved at source by reload). The model is Tier 2, so the ten-business-day escalation rule for red breaches on Tier 1 models does not apply; the red result on the 2017 snapshots was nevertheless reported to MRM on 21 May 2026 and resolved before the RDS was frozen.

documents.title: Economic downturn identification and downturn CCF – retail revolving exposures

sections.heading: Purpose and scope
sections.text: This report identifies the economic downturn for the type of exposures 'retail revolving exposures to natural persons' (qualifying revolving retail exposures within the meaning of CRR Article 142(1)(2) as a type of exposures) for the estimation of downturn conversion factors under CRR Article 182(1)(b), in accordance with Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/930. The identification was performed as of 30 September 2026 by Retail Credit Risk Modelling and is used in CCF-REV v3.0; it is separate from the downturn identification for the Bank's other types of exposures. The downturn specification is based only on historically observed economic conditions, not on hypothetical stress-test scenarios.

In addition, the consumer confidence index of Statistics Netherlands (CBS) is included as an indicator of the cycle specific to consumer credit, because it leads card spending and revolving balances. Financial credit indices are required only for exposures to institutions and are therefore not part of this indicator set.

sections.heading: Levels versus changes and most severe values
sections.text: GDP, household debt and disposable income are analysed as year-on-year growth rates, because they are reported and interpreted as growth and their levels trend upward; the unemployment rate, the BKR default rate and the loss rate are analysed in levels, because their levels reveal the cycle directly. sections.heading: Downturn periods
sections.text: Each downturn period is identified as a period in which an indicator of the relevant set reaches its most severe 12-month value. Unemployment, BKR default rate, loss rate, household debt, disposable income and consumer confidence are significantly correlated (pairwise correlations above 0.6) and reached their most severe values between 2012Q2 and 2014Q1; they are treated as one single downturn period 2012Q2–2014Q1, which is long enough to cover all related peaks and troughs. For GDP, values within 10% of the most severe value were observed only in the quarters around 2020Q2, and no adjacent trough of comparable severity relates to the same economic condition, so the downturn period equals the 12-month period 2019Q3–2020Q2; the GDP trough of 2009 (−4.4% year-on-year, 2008Q3–2009Q2) is recorded as a further candidate period. No downturn period is shorter than 12 months.

sections.heading: Impact of the downturn periods on realised CCFs
sections.text: Realised CCFs are attributed to downturn periods by their reference date, because drawings between reference date and default reflect conditions over the preceding twelve months; the quarterly average realised CCF lags the unemployment rate by two quarters (maximum cross-correlation 0.58). For reference dates in 2012Q2–2014Q1 the default-weighted realised CCF exceeds the LRA by 2.8 percentage points for credit cards and 3.1 percentage points for overdrafts, while for reference dates in 2019Q3–2020Q2 it is 1.9 percentage points below the LRA, reflecting government support and lower consumer spending during the lockdowns. The 2008–2009 period is not covered by the RDS; its impact was estimated with the regression of quarterly realised CCFs on the change in unemployment (coefficient 0.9 percentage points per percentage point, R² 0.46), giving +2.6 percentage points, below the impact observed for 2012–2014. The downturn period 2012Q2–2014Q1 is therefore the period most strongly evidenced by elevated realised CCFs.

sections.heading: Downturn CCF estimates
sections.text: The downturn add-on per pool is the difference between the default-weighted average realised CCF of reference dates in 2012Q2–2014Q1 and the LRA, floored at zero; the add-ons range from 1.5 percentage points (CC-4) to 3.6 percentage points (OD-1) and are used because they are more conservative than the LRA. The pool-level estimates are reported in MDD section 5.2. The effect of cyclical factors was separated from structural effects by comparing the 2012–2014 CCFs with those of 2015–2016 under the same limit policy: the difference disappears within two years, confirming a cyclical effect.

sections.heading: Scope
sections.text: This report documents the implementation and testing of CCF-REV v3.0 in the production environment RiskCalc (monthly pool assignment and exposure value calculation) before go-live, covering implementation testing, reconciliation with the development code, the parallel run and user acceptance testing, as required by MRM-STD-030. sections.heading: Implementation specification and data lineage
sections.text: The implementation specification IS-CCF-REV-3.0 v1.0, approved by the Model Owner on 18 December 2026 before implementation started, defines for every input the production source field and lineage (RDW month-end tables fed by the CardServ file and Core24) and identifies one difference to the development data: in production the limit is read from the daily limit table at month-end instead of the month-end account snapshot. documents.title: Model change memorandum CCF-REV v3.0 (material change, Class A)

sections.heading: Change description and rationale
sections.text: The change replaces CCF-REV v2.1 by CCF-REV v3.0 for the Bank's retail revolving exposures: the realised CCFs are measured with a twelve-month fixed horizon instead of annual cohorts, the pool structure changes from six to ten pools, an explicit downturn add-on is introduced and the MoC is re-quantified under CRM-STD-101. The objective is to comply with CRR Article 182(1)(g) and to remediate condition C-2025-044 and the validation findings V25-03 and V25-05; the planned implementation date is the first month-end after ECB permission, expected in the second quarter of 2028. The affected scope is the full range of application: 1,573,200 facilities, committed limits EUR 2,660 million, EAD EUR 1,731 million and RWEA EUR 402 million at 31 December 2026.

sections.heading: Regulatory classification
sections.text: Under Delegated Regulation (EU) No 529/2014 the change is material (Class A) because it changes the fundamental methodology for estimating conversion factors, including the downturn methodology and the MoC methodology (Annex I, Part II, Section 1, point 2(f)); it therefore requires the prior permission of the ECB under CRR Article 143(3). The change also changes the data sources for parameter estimation (addition of the daily balance history) and the composition of the time series, which on their own would require ex ante notification; they are included in the single Class A change. The change does not change the definition of default, the rating philosophy or the validation methodology, and it does not extend the range of application to new products or third-party-originated exposures. The Bank's change policy under MRM-STD-050 sets detailed criteria for classifying changes, so that classification is consistent and free of arbitrage, and was applied here.

sections.heading: Quantitative impact
sections.text: The RWEA impact was computed on the reference date 31 December 2026 with the same exposure set before and after the change, isolating the effect of the change: RWEA of the range of application increases from EUR 376 million (v2.1 without post-model adjustment) to EUR 402 million (+6.8%), and the Bank-wide credit and dilution risk RWEA at EU parent consolidated level increases by 0.08%. Because RWEA increases, the quantitative thresholds for decreases (1.5% overall, 15% and 5% for the range of application) are not met, and the classification rests on the qualitative criterion. A precise impact assessment was feasible on the full portfolio, so no sampling or inference was needed.

The application will include the confirmation, with date, of approval by the competent bodies through this internal process.

sections.heading: Other changes and notifications
sections.text: Non-material changes to the rating system, such as the annual inclusion of the latest default year in the LRA, are notified to the ECB after implementation in the quarterly aggregated ex post notification (Class C), while changes listed in Annex I, Part II, Section 2 of Delegated Regulation (EU) No 529/2014 or reducing RWEA of the range of application by at least 5% are notified at least two months before implementation (Class B). Notifications include the description and rationale, implementation date, affected scope with volumes, internal approval confirmation and, where applicable, the quantitative impact. If the Bank decides not to implement a change notified ex ante, it notifies the ECB without undue delay. Non-material changes are approved by the Model Owner after MRM has confirmed the classification, and the new version is recorded in the inventory.
